articles.title: In pictures: Brazilian President Lula da Silva
articles.summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a razor-thin runoff election that capped a deeply polarized presidential race.
articles.body: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection Sunday, defeating Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of US President Donald Trump, in a razor-thin runoff election that capped a deeply polarized presidential race.The historic victory makes the 80-year-old leftist leader the first Brazilian president to be elected to the office four times, after a campaign dominated by concerns over the cost of living, crime and corruption, as well as a broader rightward political shift in Brazil and across Latin America.It also marks the first time since the return of direct presidential elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the presidency after finishing second in the first round.Lula's mother was a seamstress and his father was an agriculture worker. Born in 1945, Lula didn't learn to read until age 10 and left school after the fifth grade to work full time. He got involved in politics because he was unhappy with the lack of political representation of the working class.

images.caption: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Brazil's president, holds a Brazilian national flag while casting a ballot at a polling station during the runoff election in Sao Bernardo do Campo, Sao Paulo state, Brazil, on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Brazilians head to the ballot box in a runoff election in which Flavio Bolsonaro and President Lula were statistically tied in a poll released on the eve of the vote. articles.title: Meet The Women Redefining Prepping As Practical Self-Care, Not Doomsday Panic
articles.summary: They’re stockpiling food, packing bugout bags, and learning survival skills—but not necessarily because they think the world is ending.

THERE'S A WELL-KNOWN maxim among preppers—particularly the small but growing subset of female preppers—that you prep for Tuesday, not doomsday. On the day I interview Krystal C. , a 37-year-old military vet turned prepping influencer in Utah, it is a Monday, and I am not prepared for that day or the one after it. That morning, I left my phone at home as I dropped my daughter off at daycare, and I haven't seen my keys—both car and home—in weeks. (I've been stealing my husband's set or simply going without.) Unlike me, Krystal has been prepping since childhood.

She learned prepping from her grandparents, although they didn't use that term. "We called it being responsible and deliberate living," Krystal says. It's a sentiment she shares with Lisa Bedford , author of the Survival Mom book and blog and de facto founding mother of the female prepper movement. "Even to this day, 17 years later, I don't really think of it as prepping," the 50-something content creator says. "I really think of it as just taking care of my family and being proactive."

Both women started seriously prepping around 2009, roughly two years before the term prepper entered mainstream consciousness. In 2011, Doomsday Preppers debuted on the National Geographic channel, and that image of preppers—predominantly white men in paramilitary garb, determined to protect their heavily armed bunkers at all costs—has endured. I spoke with 10 women for this story who all told me that while that type of prepper does exist, a more practical, family-focused approach to prepping has emerged in the 15 years since, and it's a movement led by everyday women—often the mom next door.

Even though prepping is in Krystal's DNA, she, like many others, got more serious about it after some kind of disaster. For her and Lisa, it was the Great Recession in 2008. For Zani Sunshine , a 45-year-old homesteading prepper—and one of the few highly visible Black female influencers in the prepping community—it was Hurricane Katrina and then the 2016 presidential election. Marcy R.,* another Black female prepper, started cramming her New York apartment with extra food and water after witnessing 9/11. Sue M., a 66-year-old entertainment paralegal in Los Angeles, started prepping due to the COVID-19 pandemic . For other women, like Ambrosia Luzius, a 41-year-old emergency management professional, it was not a once-in-a-lifetime disaster but the ordinary miracle of motherhood that pushed her into prepping.

Amy Edelman , 67, does not consider herself a prepper, but she did coauthor The Emergency Playbook , a how-to guide to everyday preparedness, and has a "zombie closet in the basement" filled with canned goods and vegetarian MREs (short for "meals, ready-to-eat," originally developed by the U.S. military). When Superstorm Sandy knocked out the power in Amy's house for a week, she decided to get a few more flashlights and stock some water in her basement. When inflation spiked the price of tomatoes, she went to her local garden center and bought what she needed to grow her own. She has a bugout bag (the colloquial term for the pack of essentials you prepare in order to flee your home) and knows how much it should weigh based on her body weight (15 to 20 percent). But she hasn't road-tested it by walking three times around the park yet, which is something she recommends in her book.

Despite Amy's aversion to the "prepper" title, she shares the same goal as pretty much all the other women I interviewed: "to change the reputation around prepping to something that's more lifestyle-y." She wants readers, particularly women, to realize that "you can do all this without losing your sense of normalcy."

But here's the thing: Female preppers already know that. They reject the notion that they are doing anything unusual. Instead, they see themselves as guided by ancestral common sense, rediscovering one lost art at a time, and their lives are richer—in some cases, literally—for it. The more I talked to these women, the more I realized…they may be right.

Prepping is defined as "the management of stockpiled household items in anticipation of market disruption," according to a study published in the journal Sociology . In other words, it's on us: Women are the primary shoppers for the vast majority (78 percent) of U.S. households, per Numerator, a consumer data and market research firm; and moms, in particular, do 80 percent of grocery shopping in households where a spouse or partner is present, according to Pew Research Center. They also take on more of the mental load of household management.

Women tend to be the organizers of diaper bags, the meal preppers, and the schedulers of doctor appointments, Krystal says: "This is all very natural. Women have always been caregivers and nurturers, and that sometimes gets swept to the side." In fact, it's the traits least associated with the "typical prepper" lifestyle that Krystal and other female preppers say make women arguably better suited to the task of prepping than camo-clad men doing Red Dawn cosplay. Male preppers "don't have the same pressures and responsibilities of caring for everyone on a day-to-day micro level," Zani, the homesteading prepper, says. "They may be the breadwinners, but they're not usually the ones doing the family management."

Historically, male preppers have been more visible for their focus on tactical preparedness, like combat and survivalist skills, but Lisa has been an early adopter of what's now known as "practical preparedness." This is essentially an extended version of household management that revolves around water and long-term food storage (which includes gardening , canning, and, on occasion, freeze-drying), first-aid supplies, and "everyday" activities, like practicing situational awareness. Lisa started out the way most women preppers do: buying extra shelf-stable groceries for her family. Her husband was in the construction industry during the housing crisis, and she wanted to make sure that if his business went under, their kids would still be able to eat.

The threat of food insecurity also drove Ambrosia to start prepping as a new mom. She'd just finished grad school but, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, had difficulty finding a job. So she and her family had to go on WIC for a few months. Wanting to take back control of caring for her family, she told her husband that she wanted to use 20 percent of their weekly food budget for long-term food storage. "When we did that, it changed so much for us," she says. "Here we were a family that was struggling. We were going to food pantries, and now I'm giving away food to our neighbors."

This approach continues to serve Ambrosia and her family well as they've been less affected by the supply chain issues, rising inflation, and food shortages of recent years. "If I buy flour today, it is X price. There's no arguing that tomorrow is X plus one, and next year is X plus two. So if I buy it today and my brain is thinking long-term, I'm saving myself money today, but I'm saving future-me money, too," Ambrosia says. "That's the way I've told people like, 'Hey, I'm not crazy.' I'm not preparing for a shit-hits-the-fan [SHTF] situation. I'm just preparing for the regular future with hiccups."

Black female preppers, however, are not necessarily prepping only for the occasional layoff. They're focused on societal collapse, too, Zani says. Prepping is new to her majority Black, female, and urban audience (she currently has more than half a million Instagram followers) because "there's a lot of things that we have to deal with and think about that white people do not." When you're just trying to survive amid the systemic racism and oppression of today, it's difficult to think about, much less plan for, tomorrow. Still, Zani's advice to her followers sits squarely in the practical preparedness realm. "I try to press upon them that this is not just for the end of the world," she says, but that prepping for things like job loss and natural disasters can be helpful for anyone no matter how they feel about what's going on. "If you do lose your job and you have food in your house, that's going to help you get through it better."

Long associated with Second Amendment–sponsored protection (Krystal refers to ammunition as "Freedom Seeds" in one Prepping 101 video), prepping—and most preppers—have been assumed to be politically conservative. Indeed, many are, but over the past 10 years Zani has seen a political shift among preppers. In fact, all the women I spoke to either identified as being on the liberal side of the spectrum or were careful not to share their political views. (For all of the prepping content creators, aside from Zani, it's bad for business.)

Sue even sees prepping as a way to reach across the aisle. "There's so much division and hate right now in the world, it's nice to find common ground with people," she says. "A lot of these prepper people, I suspect, have very different political views than I do, but that's not what we talk about."

Incidentally, the right to bear arms was the one political view shared by all of the women I spoke with, except for Amy, who actually advocates against gun ownership in her book. Another quality preppers tend to have in common is a general distrust of the government, Krystal says. They don't believe that the government is coming to save them when disaster strikes—or worse, they're worried that government agencies will seize their preps. "I've been doing this on social media for so long, I'll see people that are like, 'I'm prepping because Biden ran.' 'I'm prepping because Trump ran,' " she says. "I remain very apolitical.… If you're worrying about a certain scenario, prep for it."

Similarly, Des, a 30-something prepping content creator and single mom in the Northern California suburbs, doesn't "share too much" of her political views online because the way she sees it, a power outage or flash flood doesn't care who you voted for. Disaster doesn't discriminate; it impacts everyone.

But a SHTF situation wouldn't impact everyone equally . On average, Black Americans receive less Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) relief funding than white Americans, and their communities take longer to recover in the wake of natural disasters. That's why Zani isn't afraid to ruffle a few (a lot of) feathers with her political views; the stakes are too high. "As a Black woman, I can't stay silent, especially since I'm just waking up my audience and this is something that might heavily affect them," she says. Zani notes that her audience has not had the privilege to prepare because they're forced to spend the majority of their time, energy, and money simply trying to survive systemic racism and oppression. "That's why [Black] people aren't thinking about job loss, natural disasters. It's just, 'Where is this country going?' "

The urge to prep stems from uncertainty about the future. For many women, including myself, that uncertainty only amplifies when they become moms. Morgan Rogue , 42, a prepping content creator and mom of three in the Texas suburbs, sums it up perfectly: "I'm going to be prepared for anything so they don't have to go through anything."

But while many moms are interested in prepping (and have the Costco receipts to prove it), Krystal often hears from these followers that they don't know how to get started. She tells them, "Your diaper bag is already better than some guys' bugout bags." Then she encourages them to take that approach and apply it to other areas in their lives. That, in essence, is practical prepping and why women, particularly mothers, are natural-born preppers.

Morgan has involved her children with prepping "since birth" simply by doing everyday prepper activities, such as packing bugout bags, around them. Now that her kids are older, she gamifies preparedness drills, like seeing who can get out of the house with their bugout bag the fastest.

Des also uses games to pass down preparedness skills (like situational awareness) to her 7-year-old daughter. Her goal is to inspire and empower her daughter, not scare her, so she incorporates things like a prepper version of "I Spy" where she asks her daughter to spot anything that might look out of place when they're in public. Other times, she encourages her daughter to help her figure out the safest place to park. The goal is to encourage kids to be more vigilant in everyday situations, Des says.

Ambrosia also weaves in preparedness lessons and uses her garden to help teach her 5-year-old daughter where food comes from, how to grow it, and how to prepare it to last longer. She also dresses her daughter in boys' clothes because they're more "durable" and "thicker" and makes sure she's always wearing practical shoes. She teaches her children the importance of having an exit plan in place and a predetermined meeting spot to reconvene if there's an emergency.

Former New York City resident Marcy now lives "on a family compound" in South Carolina with her four adult children, their spouses, and her grandchildren. Being a mother has always impacted how she's prepped, but becoming a grandmother has recently changed her approach because she makes sure to stock extra diapers, baby formula, and infant medication. "I tried to get my children to join in, but they said I have enough food for everybody," she says. "Sometimes, it's in one ear, out the other."

Meanwhile, Sue's 31-year-old son is "not on board at all" with her prepping. "He doesn't have the worrywart mentality," she says, "so my son thinks I'm being ridiculous." Even though he doesn't live with his parents, Sue and her husband (who has gotten on board) make sure to prepare with him in mind.

"Most preppers feel lonely and isolated in their prepping because our families want nothing to do with it," says Zani. For these preppers, community—either in person or online—can be a lifeline.

Finding a Sisterhood at the End of the World

When Des started prepping in 2017, she looked for advice and, she hoped, community on social media. What she found left her feeling "a bit discouraged." At the time, Des says, the online prepping community was "extremely male-dominated" and often tinged by that trademark "gloom and doom." But the landscape is changing.

In 2022, a female-focused subreddit r/TwoXPreppers branched off from r/preppers , an ostensibly coed prepping platform where the majority of posts were nonetheless driven by male-centric concerns. Despite its biologically based name, the forum provides a trans-inclusive and pro-LGBTQIA "place where women can talk about prepping for their specific needs." A month after its creation, it had 7,500 members while the original preppers subreddit boasted 292,000. Now, r/TwoXPreppers has grown in influence—up to 33,000 weekly visitors—while r/preppers has actually shrunk to 137,000.

But prepping platforms aren't limited to Reddit. In April 2026, a small group of female preppers created the "Women Only Survival Preppers" group on Facebook. In just a few short months, more than 13,000 women (including myself) have joined. "We absolutely need a safe space, and I really think that this group is fostering that," says Storm, a 57-year-old prepper in Wabash Valley, Indiana, who joined in May.

Given Ambrosia's background in emergency management, she'd also joined prepper Facebook groups over the years. But she was especially drawn to the women-only group because it reminded her of her grandmother, who'd tried to teach her preparedness skills as a child. Ambrosia now admits she didn't really listen. "I'm trying to gather all that knowledge, and that's why I started networking with other women in prepping," she says. She sees herself as part of this "underbelly movement" of women rediscovering—and, just as important, sharing—forgotten knowledge passed down by the women who came before them. "We're kind of just relearning it together," she says. "Women are unique [in that we] don't learn something to keep it and to knowledge-hoard. I'm learning something, and that day or the next day, I'm teaching another woman."

Sue joined the group for similar reasons: "I just thought I would really like to get to know other women who are doing this," she says, adding that she admires how "self-sufficient" some of the other women are. When we speak, she's been a member of the Facebook group for less than two weeks but has already learned a lot from other women's posts, particularly about gardening and raising chickens.

Lest you think "Women Only Survival Preppers" is a virtual Lilith Fair at the end of the world, I should remind you that it is, after all, still a Facebook group, where the ordinary pitfalls of human interaction still apply. There have been controversies around LGBTQ issues, debates around abortion and vaccines ; in July, one woman was even banned for posting the address of another (a.k.a. doxxing). Still, all the women I interviewed agreed that it was better than the alternative: dealing with men.

For Marcy, the women in the female prepper Facebook groups are more mature and confident and have more common sense than men in similar groups who seem to focus on only one thing. "Everything was about weapons, weapons, weapons," she says. While firearms are part of prepping for Marcy, having a stable food supply, first-aid skills, and a strong community dynamic is more her focus.

In fact, Marcy left three coed prepper groups "because the men were out of control," she says. She often read "very degrading and disgusting" comments, and even though they weren't directed at her, she still felt attacked. Storm and Sue confirm that they've also seen no shortage of misogynistic comments in other coed online prepper spaces. Krystal doesn't even use her last name due to threats she's received online, and other content creators also talk about pushback from male followers who say that female preppers don't know what they're talking about or that they're not "real" preppers.

The women-only groups also provide a safe space for female preppers to discuss one of the biggest threats to them in SHTF scenarios: sexual violence. Storm doesn't mince words when she talks about the threat men pose to women. "Forget when shit hits the fan. Women are raped by men every day," she says. "Do I think it's going to get worse? Absolutely." The threat of men is why Sue, after "being very anti-gun for many years," recently bought a pistol and started taking shooting lessons. "I still don't think anyone needs a semiautomatic weapon, but…I also think, unfortunately, that's a skill [gun familiarity] you should have," Sue says. "[I] hope I never have to use it, but I don't want to be in a position where I wished I had learned."

While all of the women I spoke with found their positive prepping community online, Ambrosia is one of a select few with an in-person prepper group, and she's also encouraged all of her friends to prep. Krystal has friends who come over with the food they've grown, and they'll can together, and also run different drills. "Community is so important because if you want to be completely self-reliant, you're going to end up relying on others," says Krystal. "Lone wolves do not survive long."

Morgan has also held preparedness classes in her community, although it hasn't been the best place to meet fellow female preppers since the majority of attendees have been men. She's thinking about holding a women-only event because, she hypothesizes, women may be more comfortable around other women.

Planning for the Worst, Feeling Their Best

The preppers report that prepping benefits their mental health. They used words like safe , secure , grounded , optimistic , and peace of mind to describe the impact it's had on their lives. Zani, who has had depression since she was 13 (for which she currently takes medication), says she used to have "extreme anxiety all of the time" when she was working a traditional full-time job and living in a city. She was burnt out from trying to balance work responsibilities, a household budget, and child-rearing duties. Prepping and homesteading have allowed her to depend less on money, so she "can have a freer lifestyle," she says. "I very, very rarely have any anxiety whatsoever now."

Prepping may be one of the only actions that both comes from and alleviates anxiety. "Fear leads us to do some pretty productive things," says Lisa, likening prepping to getting an annual mammogram. "Not many women like going in for a breast exam—having those smooshed between metal plates doesn't feel good—but there's that little, tiny bit of risk, that little, tiny bit of fear that makes me think, Maybe I should do that ."

That was the case for Morgan, who says prepping cured her doomscrolling habit. Now, she uses that time to learn an off-grid cooking method, tend her garden, or simply go for a walk. It's made a difference for Amy too: "All I read these days is how stressed-out people are," she says. "But if you do something every day to prepare, you don't have to worry about it." In other words, if you think of prepping as a last-ditch effort to stave off the apocalypse, you're going to live your life like that. If you think of it as taking everyday action to adapt to a changing world, you're going to live your life like that.

Still, a perspective change doesn't promise an instant fix. "I am incredibly depressed about what's happening in this country," Sue says. "I don't drink; I don't do drugs. This is how I'm coping." Prepping makes her feel she's "in control," which has, on some level, alleviated her anxiety. It's also encouraged her to be a lifelong learner, which she says has benefited her brain health, especially as she's grown older. "I'm now thinking about things I have never thought about, and I have to figure out different strategies and learn how to do things I've never done before," she says.

Even just working through the mental exercise of If X happened, what would I do? has provided Des with a new level of self-confidence. "That mental exercise is sometimes all you need to feel that much more prepared if you had to respond," she says. "When an incident happens, I'm not resorting to anxiety and fear; I'm resorting to action and training."

"I'm just preparing for the worst, but hoping for the best," Marcy says. But while she's glad she's prepped so much throughout the years, she still has difficulty living her life. As one of the few single preppers I spoke with, she admits she does get lonely sometimes. Since divorcing her husband decades ago, she finds it difficult to trust anyone outside her family (it's for this reason that she chooses to comment anonymously on the women-only prepper Facebook group). "People will take your kindness for stupidity," Marcy says. "I'm not going to let you in my house. I'm not going to let you know what I have."

Des is also divorced, and although she doesn't blame the divorce on prepping, she does admit that it was a factor. "It's really hard to get other family members on board.… You usually have one person that's gung ho about it and wants to take action, and the other person needs a bit more convincing," she says. "That was the case for me. I found that the more I tried to convince [my ex-husband] we should do this, it sounded like panic." While that was not her intention, she understands how it might have come off that way, because prepping is "not the normal track for most people," she says.

Many of the women preppers I spoke with, however, said their partners were at the very least supportive of their lifestyle, and some had become more involved with prepping over the years. Some, like Sue, even said that prepping has had a positive impact on her marriage because it gave her and her husband a shared hobby: gardening. "It's a new, exciting chapter in our relationship because after you're married 32 years, you figured nothing's going to be new anymore," Sue says. Gardening has also helped Sue live a healthier life overall. Usually, when she'd get home from work, she'd flop onto the couch and watch TV. Now, she goes outside to check on her tomatoes. "It's a little way to be more active [and] get fresh air," she says.

Since starting this article , there's been a chemical leak in California, a deadly earthquake in Venezuela, flash flooding in Texas, wildfires in California, and a suspected Iranian hacking of water systems across seven states, including my own. "Most of the things that we prep for are things that happen all the time, unfortunately," Krystal says. As a millennial, she's witnessed so many "once-in-a-lifetime" events—terrorist attacks, multiple wars, a Great Recession, a global pandemic, and dozens of climate change–related natural disasters—that they've become normal. "When people say, 'You're doing all of this, and nothing's going to happen,' I'm like, 'Whoa, where have you been the last 30 years?' " Krystal says. "It's been a rough go." As a fellow millennial, I have to agree.

The more I talked to these women, the more I became convinced that some level of preparedness was necessary for my life. To customize my approach to prepping, Lisa told me to begin tracking what I was already eating and how many everyday supplies (toilet paper, laundry detergent, etc.) I used for two to three weeks. Then to ask myself: What can I do to replicate that as long as possible, using food that I can store long-term?

I'll be honest: I haven't been that methodical. I've bought a few canned goods and cases of water, dabbled in the airtight-food-storage game, started assembling bugout bags for myself, my husband, and our daughter, and taken a class in CPR and first aid.

I'm nowhere near close to having years' worth of prepped food like some women preppers, or even having a casual zombie apocalypse closet like Amy, but my meager preps have already come in handy. One weekday night, I noticed my husband opening up a can of black beans from my small but mighty prepping pantry. (I knew it was one of these cans because I'd taken to writing the expiration date on the top with a black Sharpie.) "Did you take this from my stash?" I asked him.

"Yeah, I forgot to get black beans at the store," he admitted reluctantly. "So I'm really glad we had this extra can, in case of an emergency." He was mocking me, but still, I think I made my point.

Even though we didn't need to break out the gallon-size water bottles I'd bought at Costco when it seemed like our regular water supply might be at risk, it was good to know that if we had to, we could've. And as the women preppers promised, I even started to feel a small yet significant shift in my mental health. The situation was scary, especially with a young child at home, but I felt—for lack of a better word—prepared.

And Krystal was right about diaper bags being underrated proof of women's everyday preparedness. My car keys were in there after all.

Lula (PT), por sua vez, ampliou suas vitórias de 39 para 72 cidades e recebeu mais de 2,6 milhões de votos a mais no estado em comparação com o primeiro turno. articles.body:
Mapa do estado de São Paulo com a distribuição de votos para Flávio Bolsonaro (azul) e Lula (vermelho) no segundo turno das eleições 2026. — Foto: Arte/g1

O presidente reeleito para o inédito quarto mandato, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) , ampliou de 39 para 72 o número de cidades em que venceu no estado de São Paulo no segundo turno da eleição presidencial. Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), por sua vez, foi o mais votado em 573 dos 645 municípios paulistas, ante 603 no primeiro turno.

Com isso, Lula passou de 6,05% para 11,16% dos municípios paulistas, enquanto Flávio passou de 93,49% para 88,84%. Os percentuais correspondem à proporção de cidades em que cada candidato venceu.

No segundo turno, Flávio recebeu 14.137.519 votos (53,85% dos votos válidos) em todo o estado, enquanto Lula somou 12.116.838 (46,15%). Os dados municipais mostram ainda que, embora o candidato do PL tenha vencido na maioria das cidades, o petista ampliou sua presença no mapa eleitoral paulista.

Lula recebeu mais de 2,6 milhões de votos a mais no estado em comparação com o primeiro turno, quando o petista registrou 9.505.413 votos (38,20%).

A capital paulista foi a cidade com mais votos para os dois candidatos. Lula, porém, venceu e virou em oito zonas eleitorais . Ele recebeu 3.862.401 votos (55,5%), e Flávio, 3.096.588 (44,5%) . Na comparação com o primeiro turno, o petista passou de 35 para 43 zonas eleitorais vencidas, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro recuou de 22 para 14.

Mapa da apuração em São Paulo - 2º turno — Foto: Reprodução g1

Saltinho teve maior percentual de votos para Flávio; Itapura, para Lula

A maior porcentagem de votos de Flávio Bolsonaro entre os municípios paulistas foi registrada em Saltinho, onde o candidato recebeu 80,22% dos votos, o equivalente a 4.718. Lula teve 1.163 votos (19,78%) na cidade.

Já Lula teve seu maior percentual em Itapura, com 68,61% dos votos, ou 1.845. Flávio recebeu 844 votos (31,39%) no município.

Outras cidades em que Flávio obteve percentuais elevados foram Marapoama, com 76,63%, e Itajobi, com 74,31%.

Entre os municípios com maior percentual de Lula, depois de Itapura, estão Sandovalina, com 62,94%, e Euclides da Cunha Paulista, com 62,61%.

Duas cidades tiveram diferença de apenas um voto

A disputa mais apertada entre os dois candidatos ocorreu em São João do Pau d'Alho e Nova Luzitânia. A diferença foi de apenas um voto em cada município.

Em São João do Pau d'Alho, Lula recebeu 769 votos (50,03%), contra 768 de Flávio Bolsonaro (49,97%). Já em Nova Luzitânia, Flávio teve 1.039 votos (50,02%), enquanto Lula somou 1.038 (49,98%).

Outras disputas tiveram diferenças pequenas. Em Serra Azul, Flávio venceu por seis votos: 2.884 (50,05%) a 2.878 (49,95%). Em Guatapará, Lula ficou à frente por sete votos, com 2.127 (50,08%) contra 2.120 (49,92%).

Também houve uma diferença de oito votos em Brejo Alegre, onde Flávio recebeu 1.076 votos (50,19%) e Lula, 1.068 (49,81%). Em Motuca, Lula venceu por dez votos: 1.336 (50,19%) a 1.326 (49,81%).

Apesar das disputas apertadas, não houve empate em nenhum dos 645 municípios paulistas no segundo turno. No primeiro turno, porém, Trabiju registrou empate, com 574 votos para cada candidato . Neste domingo, Lula venceu na cidade com 664 votos (52,04%), contra 612 (47,96%) de Flávio Bolsonaro.

articles.title: Brazil’s Lula wins re-election, defeating Trump ally Bolsonaro
articles.summary: Brazil’s president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected after defeating conservative challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s presidential runoff, the
articles.body: Brazil’s president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected after defeating conservative challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s presidential runoff, the country’s electoral authority announced, keeping Latin America’s largest economy under left-wing leadership.With more than 78% of votes counted, Lula was leading with 51.21% against Bolsonaro’s 48.79%, according to Reuters’ live election coverage. Pollster Datafolha projected Lula to win before the electoral authority confirmed his victory.The result is a setback for US President Donald Trump’s allies in Latin America. A Bolsonaro victory would have marked a rightward shift in Brazil, the region’s most populous country and largest economy, while Lula’s win leaves Brazil and Mexico with left-of-centre leaders.Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator and son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, had campaigned on closer ties with Washington and promised to secure better deals with the Trump administration. Lula had criticised US policies towards Brazil, including tariffs on Brazilian exports and the designation of drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organisations.The contest pitted two sharply polarised political camps against each other, with differences spanning relations with the United States, crime, climate policy and social welfare. Lula, who previously governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010, had sought an unprecedented fourth term.Lula supporters celebrate victoryLula supporters celebrated as the results showed him pulling ahead. Reuters reported World Cup-like scenes in Rio de Janeiro’s Laranjeiras neighbourhood, where people gathered in bars to follow the count and began singing as Lula overtook Bolsonaro.In downtown São Paulo, supporters at a nightclub cheered the news of Lula’s projected win.“I’ve been optimistic about Lula winning since the first round, even with Flávio in the lead,” Lucas dos Santos, a 29-year-old biomedical scientist, told Reuters.Julia Bueno, a 28-year-old technology worker, said she had attended a rally for Lula on Saturday and wanted to be near Avenida Paulista so she could join celebrations as soon as his victory was announced.“I was at the Saturday rally, and it was so moving. Seeing him right in front of us was an indescribable feeling,” she told Reuters.Supreme Court extends voting by two hoursVoting was extended nationwide by two hours after Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin issued an order shortly after polls were due to close. Both candidates had sought extensions in some areas, but for different reasons: Lula cited problems with buses transporting voters in nine states, while Bolsonaro pointed to heavy rain in the south.The order raised logistical concerns because some polling stations had already closed. In Brasilia, volunteers overseeing the count debated whether they needed to remain after the announcement. At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, voting machines had been switched off and could not be restarted, according to the Associated Press.Bolsonaro had led Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round earlier this month. More than 33 million of Brazil’s nearly 160 million voters had not turned out.The runoff was a rematch between two political forces that have divided the country. Lula defeated Jair Bolsonaro by the narrowest margin since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1985 in the previous presidential election four years ago.Cost of living and security shape campaignLula faced a difficult re-election battle amid voter concerns over rising living costs and crime. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime platform central to his campaign and promised to lower food prices, while Lula offered costly incentives in an effort to win over undecided voters.Both camps have faced corruption allegations involving allies and family members. Bolsonaro has been implicated in a sprawling scandal, while Lula spent more than a year in prison after corruption convictions that were later annulled.As Bolsonaro voted at a school in Rio de Janeiro, supporters shouted, “Lula, thief, your place is in prison,” while Lula’s supporters chanted in his favour.“The time of real change has arrived,” Bolsonaro said before the result. “Brazil can’t go on for another four years on its current trajectory.”Lula’s supporters said they backed him because of his record of supporting marginalised communities and reducing poverty.“Lula is a man of the people and he knows what it’s like to be poor,” Luzia da Souza, who runs a bar in Rio de Janeiro, told AP. “I find it impossible not to vote for him.”Anderson Falcão, a 43-year-old journalist in Brasilia, said he was concerned about Bolsonaro’s long-term political vision, which he described as “exclusionary”.“It’s a project that harms the less fortunate, harms the worker, women, the forest, the Amazon,” he said.Bolsonaro supporters, many wearing Brazil’s yellow and green jerseys, said they wanted change. Fabianne Borges Santoro, a 45-year-old physiotherapist in Rio de Janeiro, said prices were high and taxes too steep. She added that she had previously voted for Lula’s party but now associated it with corruption.Trump administration looms over electionThe Trump administration’s approach to Brazil became a central issue in the campaign. Lula criticised Trump over tariffs imposed on Brazilian exports and the US designation of drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organisations. Experts said the measures may have been intended to portray Lula as weak on crime.Flávio Bolsonaro highlighted his ties to the White House and argued that Brazil needed better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare-earth minerals sector. Brazil estimates that it holds deposits of up to 21 million tonnes, second only to China. Bolsonaro denied receiving assistance from the US government.Trump said on Sunday that he was following the election but declined to endorse either candidate.You use AI every day. articles.title: Conservative wave hits roadblock in Brazil as Lula holds off Bolsonaro challenge
articles.summary: In a tight election, incumbent President Lula da Silva bested Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil.
articles.body: Incumbent leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva narrowly defeated conservative Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro in Sunday's presidential runoff, according to The Associated Press. The deeply polarized nation returned to the polls for a second round runoff on Sunday. Despite trailing by nearly 4.4 million votes, Bolsonaro has yet to concede defeat. Lula addressed supporters after winning reelection, expressing gratitude to the Brazilian people. "No one is required to like the president-elect, but he must govern for everyone," Lula said. BRAZIL BECOMES NEXT TEST FOR LATIN AMERICA’S SURGING CONSERVATIVE MOVEMENT Referring to his opponent, Lula said, "This was a defeat for denialism and lies." Lula’s victory followed chaos at polling places after a Supreme Court justice ordered a last-minute, two-hour voting extension, a move that could face a legal challenge from Bolsonaro. While the Flavio Bolsonaro campaign had also requested an extension in certain areas impacted by heavy rains, the unusual decision by the court to extend voting hours nationwide by two hours will certainly draw scrutiny. Lula petitioned for the extension, claiming that buses were not circulating to take voters to the polls as expected. "I've never complained about anything in any election before. Whether I won or lost, I'd just accept it and get ready for the next one. But this time, something abominable is happening," Lula argued. The Bolsonaro camp is likely to claim that the extension favored Lula. Bolsonaro narrowly won the first round on Oct. 4, with 47% of the vote, to Lula's 45%, but fell short of the 50% majority required to win the election outright. The victory marks an unprecedented fourth presidential term for Lula, and a remarkable comeback victory. The result is even more surprising given that Bolsonaro had led, albeit by tight margins, in recent polling, and Brazil had recently elected a conservative congress aligned with the Bolsonaro agenda. BRAZIL’S RAPID ELECTION COUNT PUTS SPOTLIGHT ON VOTING SECURITY AHEAD OF US MIDTERMS Earlier in the day, Lula voted in Sao Bernardo do Campo, Sao Paulo, while Bolsonaro voted in the north of Rio de Janeiro, the state he represents in the Senate. The first vote tallies came in from Brazilians living overseas, where Lula won a decisive victory in Germany, and Bolsonaro won an overwhelming victory in Japan. While Bolsonaro performed well in his southern electoral strongholds, winning by comfortable margins in Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Paraná, and Rio Grande do Sul, he won those states by smaller margins than in the first round. His turnout in the south was not enough to overcome Lula's famed Northeastern firewall; a reflection of the Workers Party dominance in the country's populous "Nordeste" region. Bolsonaro also turned in a disappointing performance in Minas Gerais, which geographically and politically straddles the Brazilian north/south divide. Often referred to as the nation's quintessential bellwether state, it is fair to say that as goes Minas Gerais, so goes the nation. While Bolsonaro won Minas Gerais by 5% in the first round, in the second round it was essentially tied. Bolsonaro had received endorsements from other first round candidates: best-selling author Augusto Cury, former Minas Gerais Governor Romeu Zema, and former Goiás Governor Ronaldo Caiado. LATIN AMERICA’S CONSERVATIVE SHIFT FACES ITS BIGGEST TEST YET IN BRAZIL ELECTION However, they were not enough to overcome the much-respected electoral machinery of the Workers Party. Lula has now appeared on the presidential ballot 7 times, winning 4 of those elections. Heading into the first round, Flavio Bolsonaro was effectively able to make the case to working-class and middle-class voters that the Lula's economic approach was driving up their cost of living. He painted the Lula administration as bloated, tax-heavy, and given to racking up debt and tied this to inflation and kitchen table economics. Additionally, his message of hardline law and order appealed to a Brazilian public where voters routinely suggest that violence is the most pressing issue. Nonetheless, these economic and security concerns were not enough to overcome a generation of loyalty to the Workers Party and its social programs, particularly in the North and Northeast of the country, where Lula won by wide margins. While Lula will be riding high heading into a historic fourth term in office, he will face a Congress with a center-right and right-wing majority that has been described as one of the most conservative in history. While Flavio Bolsonaro lost the 2026 election by a narrow margin, the Bolsonaro movement is certainly not going away, and arguably remains an influential force in modern Brazilian politics. The Lula victory also brings to an end a long string of victories for Trump-backed right-wing candidates across the region. While Trump had not officially endorsed Flavio Bolsonaro, he made no secret of his preference, and enjoyed a close relationship with the Bolsonaro family. Looking forward to 2030, all eyes will turn to Bolsonaro clan ally Tarcisio de Freitas, who stepped aside this election cycle, in order to clear the way for Flavio Bolsonaro's run. Will the Brazilian right back another Bolsonaro in four years time, or will the popular São Paulo governor also mount a bid? Bolsonaro-aligned candidates appeared poised to win most of those races. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Israel drills for surprise attack with massive military exercise as expert invokes 1973 war
articles.summary: Israel's largest military drill in years mobilizes multiple divisions to counter border infiltrations, as an analyst invokes the 1973 Yom Kippur War.
articles.body: The Israeli military launched large-scale domestic military exercises on Sunday to counter surprise border infiltrations and ground raids across northern and central Israel, mobilizing multiple divisions and air assets amid rising regional tensions. The drills, set to continue over 48 hours, came as an Israeli security expert invoked the 1973 Yom Kippur War, when Egypt and Syria used exercises to disguise preparations for a surprise attack, warning that escalating tensions in the region could in fact trigger what he described as a "dangerous miscalculation." The large-scale maneuvers, the IDF said, involve the Northern Command’s 210th Division, the West Bank Division, and the Central Command’s 98th and 96th divisions, alongside the Israeli Air Force. IRAN TARGETS US WITH PSYCHOLOGICAL WARFARE CAMPAIGN TO MANIPULATE AMERICANS, EMBARRASS TRUMP: EXPERTS The exercise, scheduled just ahead of Israel's elections Oct. 27, aims to "maintain the forces’ alertness and readiness, strengthen the ability to defend communities, and make full use of aerial capabilities for defense in the area," according to the IDF. On Friday, the IDF said troops would practice "a variety of scenarios, including a surprise attack and infiltration into Israeli territory by air and land," incorporating lessons learned from the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel. "This exercise is mostly about non-state actors with or without Iranian support," Israeli national security analyst Dr. Ehud Eilam told Fox News Digital. "It's aimed at those in Syria, Lebanon, and Jordan who might try to infiltrate into Israel or send ground raids. Some are supported by Iran; others are not. It could be planned by Iran or be a local initiative." NETANYAHU PRAISES TRUMP'S 'WICKED SENSE OF HUMOR,' DEFENDS IRONCLAD ALLIANCE AHEAD OF HISTORIC ISRAEL VOTE "This is a massive exercise, the biggest one in recent years, aimed at protecting the borders," the former Israeli Ministry of Defense researcher added. "It's all about making sure that the election day on October 27 will run smoothly. It's also a message to Iran and others: don't try to provoke us during election day, so nothing will be disrupted." The Israeli drills followed a show of force by Tehran days earlier, during which the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) fired roughly 30 ballistic missiles across two distinct weapon classes, according to reports. That live-fire display highlighted Iranian strike capabilities and sparked renewed alerts about commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and prompted the Israeli military to heighten its alert level while maintaining maximum readiness for a targeted strike against Iran. TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME During a visit to the IDF's Central Command on Wednesday, Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir warned that the risk of escalation was growing. "Given the numerous warnings across all fronts and the sensitivity of the current period, the potential for escalation has increased," Zamir said. "To ensure better operational control on the ground, we have reinforced our troop deployments across all sectors, including moving the 98th Division into the area to strengthen security and stability." "Part of mutual deterrence: a few days ago, Iran had their own pretty big exercise, and that was actually more intimidating as far as Israel is concerned because they launched missiles and prepared for a war with Israel," Eilam said. "This exercise on Sunday and Monday is against Iran's proxies and allies at the border of Israel." Sunday’s Israeli drill also followed an Oct. 19 mission in which Israeli fighter jets and aerial refueling tankers flew 800 miles across Syrian and Iraqi airspace to Iran’s border. FROM INTELLIGENCE SHARING TO MISSILE DEFENSE, HOW ISRAEL'S PARTNERSHIP PROTECTS AMERICAN SECURITY Washington was notified in advance and viewed the maneuver as a non-kinetic show of force following the postponement of a broader strike package earlier in the month. Despite the deterrence signals, Eilam warned that large-scale military exercises carry the "risk of miscalculation" and particularly when troop movements could be mistaken for preparations for an attack. "During the Cold War, every time the Soviet Union or NATO carried out a major drill, having so many troops in the field meant they might attack if that was the intention," Eilam said. He pointed to the 1973 Yom Kippur War, when Egypt and Syria used military exercises to help conceal troop buildups along Israel's borders. Israeli intelligence largely dismissed the movements as routine drills, allowing the two countries to achieve strategic surprise when they launched a coordinated, two-front attack on Yom Kippur. TRUMP SAYS NETANYAHU NEEDS TO BE RE-ELECTED, OR ELSE US WILL HAVE TO 'FINISH THE JOB’ AGAINST IRAN ALONE "The classic example in Israel is 1973, when Egypt and Syria conducted a major exercise just before the war that turned into the actual attack," the analyst said. "Israel and Iran are now watching each other very closely and both sides suspect the other might strike first," Eilam added before stating that there is the chance of what they call "miscalculation — that each side suspects the other and strikes first by mistake." "It's all about sending messages to each other." "It remains uncertain whether there will eventually be an Israeli attack on Iran because it depends on U.S. authorization," Eilam concluded. articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Budget tax reprieve for pensioners' and 'Meghan dad net to widen'
articles.summary: Stories about the Budget and the investigation into the father of the Duchess of Sussex  feature on Monday's front pages.
articles.body:
The Times reports that the tax free allowance will be increased for low-income pensioners in Wednesday's Budget. It says the chancellor has also decided not to to reduce the tax-free pension lump sum - and quotes the former minister Steve Webb as saying this looks like a "decidedly pensioner-friendly" Budget. The i paper says John Healey will announce long-term borrowing to fund defence on Wednesday, but defer the commitment to increase the expenditure to 3% of GDP to next year's spending review.

"This budget is Andy Burnham's first real test" writes Sharon Graham, the union Unite's general secretary, in the Daily Mirror. She says "hope will soon evaporate unless there is real change that workers and communities feel".

Meanwhile, the Daily Telegraph says John Healey is at odds with the energy secretary over drilling at the Rosebank North Sea oil field. According to the paper, Healey wants the plans to go ahead, but Miatta Fahnbulleh is opposed. The paper says she is minded to object to the plan because most of the oil would have to be exported, making it less effective at addressing UK energy security.

The Guardian says it has spoken to the interior minister of the Philippines and that he says the signs are that Thomas Markle could be a "possible sex offender of the grossest kind". The minister adds that an investigation into the Duchess of Sussex's father will provide a "definitive picture". Thomas Markle has denied all the allegations against him. The Daily Mail splashes with the interview on its front page and the Sun reports it too, as well as new details from the letter sent to the Met Police in 2019 making allegations against Markle.

The British Library is "turning the page" on some of its reading rooms, according to the Times. It says the rooms are "the rarest of things in London, a sanctuary of silence" - but that three which are dedicated to science are closing permanently, and being turned into "flexible workspaces". The library's chief executive says many studies are now available online, but one professor calls it "a sad day for science".

The paper says John Healey is expected to protect about one million low-income pensioners from paying income tax by raising their tax-free allowance, adding he has also decided against reducing the amount of pension that can be taken as a tax-free lump sum.

articles.title: Satish Acharya, Manjul: India's cartoonists built an audience online - now their posts are being restricted
articles.summary: Indian cartoonists say online restrictions are making satire harder, but they aren't giving up.
articles.body:
For the second time in three weeks, Indian cartoonist Satish Acharya found himself effectively invisible on Instagram in his own country.

The 55-year-old discovered on Tuesday that his account had once again been briefly blocked in India, allegedly with no explanation from the platform.

Just a few weeks ago, another cartoonist, Manjul, had found that Instagram had restricted a post criticising India's election commission over its controversial revision of voter rolls. His profile remained accessible.

The cases have raised concerns about the use of legal orders to restrict political satire in India, with cartoonists saying they are often given little explanation for why their work has been blocked.

Acharaya's account was first restricted from 28 September to 6 October, when users in India could neither find his profile through search nor access it through a web link.

Anyone trying to access his profile saw a message saying it was unavailable under India's Information Technology Rules.

The rules allow authorities and courts to order social media platforms to remove or restrict content.

The government says they help tackle unlawful material, but artists and free-speech advocates warn they can stifle India's rich tradition of political satire.

"Meta platforms have been restricting the reach of my cartoons for some years," Acharya told the BBC. "But when my entire profile was restricted in India, I was a little sad."

He wrote to Meta, Instagram's parent company, but received no reply. He says he was preparing to go to court when his account became accessible again in early October, only to be blocked again earlier this week for three days.

In a statement, Meta told the BBC that it may temporarily restrict accounts to comply with India's IT Rules but did not explain the specific reasons for restricting Acharya's account or Manjul's post.

Critics say the restrictions come as humour and satire play an increasingly visible role in political dissent in India, particularly among younger people.

Memes and Gen-Z humour helped fuel protests over education and jobs in July, which led to the resignation of India's education minister. Online debate has also intensified over a controversial revision of voter rolls that removed 130 million names.

The political significance of social media has not been lost on the government. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has urged minister s to strengthen their online presence and connect with younger audiences.

At the same time, technology policy expert Prateek Waghre says the government is increasingly using legal orders to regulate online content.

The Indian Express reported that government agencies sent nearly 195,000 blocking and content-restriction orders to platforms including Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July through the federal government's Sahyog portal.

The figures, obtained through a right-to-information request, do not show how many posts were ultimately restricted or removed. The BBC has not seen the original response.

Waghre says that some platforms, particularly Meta, "seem more willing to comply", he says, while X appears more willing to push back. But limited public data makes comparisons difficult. Meta declined to comment on his assessment.

The government has also reportedly sought greater scrutiny of how social media platforms recommend content.

Earlier this week, several media outlets reported that authorities had asked Meta to ensure its systems did not steer users towards "a single or limited set of narratives" and strengthen checks on content that could "cause public disorder or incite violence".

The BBC has sought comment from India's IT ministry on the restrictions and reported instructions to Meta but has not received a response.

Of course, political satire has a long history in India - as do attempts to curb it.

Cartoons have been a fixture of Indian journalism since independence, with RK Laxman 's Common Man becoming one of its most recognisable characters.

But cartoonists have also faced censorship. During the Emergency in the 1970s, when civil liberties were suspended and the press was tightly controlled, Abu Abraham continued drawing, even as dozens of his cartoons were stamped "not passed by censors".

In 2012, cartoonist Aseem Trived i was arrested on sedition charges over cartoons allegedly mocking the Indian constitution. The charges were later dropped.

Today, concerns about restrictions on political expression extend beyond cartoonists. India ranks 157th in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, while critics accuse the government of putting growing pressure on independent media. The government rejects the criticism, saying India's media remains free and vibrant.

Comedians have also faced controversy over political satire. Kunal Kamra , known for his jokes about Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his party, has faced threats, cancelled shows and legal action.

For cartoonists, however, challenging those in power is central to their work.

"We are among the default opposition," says Sandeep Adhwaryu, a cartoonist at a leading Indian newspaper.

"The nature of the craft is to oppose," he says, adding that cartoonists, like journalists, must question whoever holds power.

Acharya says he has followed that principle throughout his career. Before 2014, many of his cartoons targeted the Congress-led government and were shared by BJP leaders.

"I never faced official restrictions on my cartoons during the previous governments, though there would be some trolling occasionally," he says.

Now, with the BJP in power, much of his satire is directed at Modi's government.

Social media has allowed independent cartoonists like Acharya to reach audiences without relying on newspapers or other traditional outlets.

"We are not associated with newspapers or any mainstream media. That's why we can draw," says Manjul.

But that freedom comes with a new vulnerability - dependence on platforms that can restrict their work or cut off access to their audiences.

No one knows this better than Rachita Taneja, the creator of the hugely popular Instagram comic Sanitary Panels.

"My career would not have existed without the internet," she told the BBC. Yet she describes social media as a double-edged sword.

"At the end of the day it's a for-profit endeavour that answers to advertisers," she says.

Taneja says that Meta's compliance with Indian government requests reflects the company's commercial priorities rather than concern for users' rights. Meta declined to comment.

Even cartoonists working in traditional newsrooms face pressure. Adhwaryu says artists may soften captions, avoid certain subjects or think twice before submitting a cartoon. Over time, he says, such self-censorship can become normalised, even without explicit instructions.

Still, cartoonists have found ways to support one another.

When Acharya's Instagram account was first restricted, Taneja drew a stick-figure cartoon in solidarity. "Seeing people on the front lines creating communities, protesting, running campaigns, tirelessly fighting for their own rights and the rights of others is what keeps me going," she says.

Adhwaryu believes satire will continue to adapt. He compares cartoons and humour to a "shape-shifting virus".

"It keeps mutating in response to its environment," he says. "It will find its way."

articles.title: Saudi’s Riyadh airport reopens despite renewed Houthi threats
articles.summary: Riyadh’s main airport reopened to international flights on Sunday after a two-week shutdown, even as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s capital continued
articles.body: Riyadh’s main airport reopened to international flights on Sunday after a two-week shutdown, even as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s capital continued over the weekend.Dozens of flights left King Khalid International Airport Sunday for destinations including London, Dubai and Beijing, according to the airport’s website. Local carriers Saudia and Flynas operated services, while Air India and Emirates were also listed. However, many international airlines continued to suspend operations, leaving traffic into and out of Riyadh heavily restricted. At least two of airport’s five terminals were operating. Terminal 3, damaged in strikes this month, remained closed.Airport had suspended operations after Houthi attacks on Oct 10-11 killed more than a dozen people and injured hundreds.Reopening came amid Houthi strikes on Riyadh over the weekend. Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said they intercepted a ballistic missile and drone launched towards Riyadh on Sunday. It also said it fought off a barrage of projectiles in areas near the Yemeni border.Saudi Arabia issued weekend air-raid alerts for Riyadh, Yanbu, Jeddah and Mecca. Saudi stocks fell as much as 3.4% on Sunday amid increased geopolitical risk. Gulf Cooperation Council secretary general Jasem Albudaiwi condemned the Houthi attacks endangering Mecca, calling it “a highly dangerous violation of the sanctity of the holy sites and a provocation to the sentiments of Muslims worldwide”. articles.title: Sharon Osbourne: 'I visit Ozzy's grave every day'
articles.summary: The TV presenter says she can see Ozzy's burial site from her window, and regularly talks to him.
articles.body:
It's been 15 months since Ozzy Osbourne died, at the age of 76, at his home in Buckinghamshire.

Although he had suffered from health problems for years, including Parkinson's disease and a fractured vertebra, his death was a shock.

Less than three weeks beforehand, he had been on stage in Birmingham, playing a triumphant farewell concert.

"He was just so, so happy," recalls his wife Sharon.

"He was online, going through the reviews and saying, 'There's something terribly wrong', and I'm like, 'Why?'

"He goes, 'I didn't get slagged by anybody. Why are people being nice to me?'

"And I'm like, 'Because they like you'."

On the morning he died, Ozzy had woken up early and gone downstairs for his usual morning workout. Shortly afterwards, he had a heart attack. An air ambulance was called and paramedics tried to save him. But it was too late.

"We'd spoken in the night. Ozzy had woken in the night and he asked me to kiss him twice, and I did.

"And then he said, 'Hold me, hold me tight,' and I did.

"And then the next thing I know, it's early in the morning, and someone comes rushing into the room saying, 'Come down now'.

"You've lost the love of your life, so you don't just wake up and go, 'I'm fine now. I'm cured'.

"You never get over it. But you learn to live with it, and that's what I'm trying to do. So you either sit in a room and don't come out, or you accept it, befriend it, and that's it."

The affection among Ozzy's fans was apparent before the singer's funeral. Thousands of people lined the streets of Birmingham, laying floral tributes and singing Black Sabbath songs as Ozzy's body was transported through his home city in a hearse topped by a purple floral tribute in the shape of a cross.

Sharon says he would have been mystified by the outpouring of love.

"He'd have been like, 'What's the matter with you guys? Go home!'" she says.

But for the family, the public response was a huge source of comfort.

Daughter Kelly said last year: "I never could have imagined it to be as helpful as it has been to know that we're not alone in our grief and our sadness, and that the rest of the world loved him as much as we did."

Sharon says the fans' cards and messages were all collected, sorted and photographed; while the flowers were composted for the family garden, where Ozzy is buried.

"There was no way I could put Ozzy in a public graveyard," she says.

"I've seen what happens to other people in the public eye. There's no peace because people want to come and they want to pay their respects. That's an ongoing thing, and I wanted Ozzy to rest and just be."

"Of course, every day. I can see him from my window."

She still talks to him regularly, she says. Asked what she discusses, she puts a finger to her lips and gives a gentle "shh".

Ozzy and Sharon's relationship spanned more than 50 years.

They met in 1970 and married in 1982. Their time together could be turbulent - he was arrested for attempting to murder her in 1989 (she dropped the charges), and they split briefly in 2016 amid rumours of infidelity - but the couple maintained that they were soulmates.

"It was an unusual relationship because we had such highs and such terrible lows," she admits. But at the end of his life, "he knew" how much he was loved.

You can see proof of that love - from his family, his fans and his bandmates – in a new documentary about his final gig at Birmingham's Villa Park last year, when he reunited with heavy rock legends Black Sabbath.

Titled Back To The Beginning, it features more than 25 of the songs played at that star-studded concert, including Ozzy's solo set and Sabbath's entire performance.

In backstage footage, fellow A-list performers discuss the star's influence in awestruck tones.

"If there was no Sabbath, there's no Metallica," says the band's frontman James Hetfield. "It's as simple as that."

Yungblud, whose version of Changes was one of the concert's emotional high points, talks about how, as a kid who didn't fit in, Ozzy changed his life.

"The fact he was celebrated for his madness and his individuality gave me hope."

Sharon says the concert was Ozzy's final wish: the one thing that would make him happy after years of deteriorating health.

Six months before the show, Ozzy fell and fractured his vertebrae. In recovery, he caught pneumonia three times. After surgery on his back, he caught sepsis and nearly died.

Two weeks before the show, doctors urged him to call it off.

"They came to see us at the house and they said, 'You can't do this. We're advising you not to do this. Your heart's too weak'," Sharon recalls.

But the singer was determined to see it through. In the film, it's hard to believe he's so ill. Although he performs seated on a throne, his eyes are full of life and his voice is powerful. As he looks out at the crowd, he seems elated.

Backstage, Sharon admits, "the whole family was terrified". But something changed when Ozzy entered the stadium.

"He was sat in his dressing room, watching everybody on a screen performing, and he was like, 'I just can't believe they're all here'.

"It's amazing what support and love and determination can do for you, because [before the show] he was somebody that couldn't breathe. He had a lung condition. He had a heart condition. He had terrible, terrible agony from his spine. He had blood clots and he had Parkinson's.

"Some days just to even talk was an effort, let alone sing. And I don't know how he did it, but he did it.

"And you saw it in his eyes, in his face. It just made him feel like he was alive again."

The effect was so galvanising that, when he came off stage, Ozzy declared he wanted to go on tour.

"He was raring to go," Sharon laughs. "He was like, 'I can do this, and the fans don't mind if I'm sat down'."

It's an incredible and rare thing, I suggest, to be able to grant your partner their last wish.

Ozzy may have suffered immense pain in his final years, but he was able to say goodbye in style.

"To quote one of his songs, he was flying high again," Sharon says.

"He was just floating for those last 17 days. It was great. It was joyous."

articles.title: College homecoming party turns to chaos as deck collapses, leaving at least 28 people injured
articles.summary: A back deck collapsed during a William & Mary homecoming party in Williamsburg, Virginia, injuring at least 28 people at an off-campus home.
articles.body: A college homecoming party took a frightening turn Friday night when a back deck collapsed at a Virginia home, leaving at least 28 people injured and sending emergency crews rushing to the neighborhood. William & Mary confirmed students were among those injured at the off-campus residence in Williamsburg. All reported injuries were non-life-threatening, according to city officials. Dispatchers received a report of a structure collapse around 10:07 p.m. on the 200 block of Matoaka Court. Responding police and firefighters found the home’s back deck had collapsed, the city said. TERRIFYING SCENE UNFOLDS AS METAL CABANA FRAME CRASHES INTO PACKED CASINO POOL AREA Emergency crews took 13 people to hospitals, while another 15 reportedly sought treatment on their own, according to the city’s Saturday morning update. Neighbors told WAVY that a homecoming party was underway when the deck gave way. One described emergency vehicles stretching through the neighborhood. "All the way down the street and wrapped around just ambulances and fire trucks," the neighbor, who asked not to be named, told WAVY. "We saw a lot of hospital gurneys coming out of ambulances. At least nine ambulances kind of wrapped around the street." WATCH: VIRGINIA COPS CRAWL THROUGH BURNING HOUSE TO SAVE MAN TRAPPED IN FIRE Joshua Wise, who lives next to the home, told the outlet some of his classmates were involved. He returned after emergency crews had finished responding but learned his housemate had been helping people get home. "Word was traveling pretty fast," Wise told WAVY. "By the time I got back here, the emergency response was over, but I had a housemate who was helping people, trying to help out as much as possible, drive people home, get people where they needed to be." Wise credited neighbors with coming together after the frightening incident. "We did everything we could to help each other out and I think that that’s beautiful," he said. 5 VICTIMS RELEASED FROM HOSPITAL AFTER FLORIDA A&M UNIVERSITY SHOOTING, 1 REMAINS CRITICAL In a Saturday message to the campus community, William & Mary’s senior vice president for student affairs and public safety, Ginger Ambler, said the university was still gathering information. Additional students may have sought care beyond those initially counted, she noted. "We are grateful that none of the injuries were life-threatening," Ambler wrote. She said staff across the university’s health, academic and student support offices were working to assist affected students. "We recognize that such an experience may affect our students deeply and in different ways," Ambler wrote. Wise also praised the emergency response. "Thank goodness for the emergency responders," he told WAVY. "They were great. The ambulances and everything got here pretty fast." articles.title: Two storms slam northern Europe, cut power to 150,000 homes
articles.summary: Storms Boelo and Austen kill a man in Scotland and cut electricity to homes in the UK, France and Germany.
articles.body:
A pair of storms battering northern Europe have killed one man, cut power to more than 150,000 homes, and disrupted flights and phone networks.

More than 82,000 homes in the United Kingdom, nearly 60,000 in France, and at least 10,000 in Germany had no electricity on Sunday after storms Boelo and Austen passed through the region within 24 hours, according to authorities in the countries.

A falling tree killed a man, 60, in southwestern Scotland on Sunday, while another falling tree injured two women in central Scotland, the Press Association reported.

Winds of up to 135 km/h (84 mph) were recorded in the Argyll and Bute regions of western Scotland. Trees and power cables brought down by the storm blocked roads and rail lines across Scotland and northern England.

In Brighton, on England’s southern coast, Austen blew away an unused pier on Friday.

Authorities have warned of flood risk in regions of both Scotland and England.

The Met Office, the UK’s national forecaster, warned that Boelo would bring a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves and said people should stay indoors as much as possible.

Across the English Channel, Europe battled its first big storm of the autumn, with strong winds inflicting widespread power cuts.

French energy company Enedis said that at Austen’s peak on Saturday, some 288,000 homes had no electricity. Some 59,000 remained without power at midday Sunday, mainly in Normandy and Brittany.

A marathon runner in the midst of a race in northern France was lightly injured by a tree knocked over in strong winds.

In Germany, Austen cut power to 10,000 homes in and around the southwestern town of Freiburg-Breisgau on Sunday. The town’s main hospital said it had to limit service to emergency cases because of the blackout, which also cut the mobile phone network.

German police said two people were seriously hurt on Saturday by scaffolding blown away by Austen’s strong winds at a market in the town of Nastatten.

The storms also hit the Netherlands and Belgium, where falling trees injured four people in Brussels on Saturday.

In the Netherlands, north of the island of Schiermonnikoog, three crew members on board a freight ship were injured in the storms, according to the country’s coastguard. Two of them were winched off and taken by helicopter to a hospital on the mainland.

The storms caused hundreds of flights to be cancelled or diverted across northern Europe, including at Amsterdam’s Schiphol airport, one of the continent’s busiest hubs.

Experts have warned of more extreme weather events due to climate change.

articles.title: Seoul ‘fabricated’ landmine blast, North Korea tells UN in letter
articles.summary: South Korea blames Pyongyang for September landmine blast, but North Korea says incident a ‘sinister obstructive move’.
articles.body:
Pyongyang has sent a letter to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) accusing Seoul of fabricating a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers, according to North Korea’s Korean Central News Agency.

The North Korean permanent representative to the UN wrote to the UNSC on Sunday regarding the “provocation the ROK [Republic of Korea] committed by groundlessly shifting the blame for the dubious ‘mine explosion incident’”, warning that violations of the country’s sovereignty could trigger self-defence.

Tensions have intensified after South Korea blamed a September 21 explosion in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) separating the two countries on North Korean landmines. North Korea has rejected the accusations.

Pyongyang’s UN representative alleged the landmine incident was “a sinister obstructive move to brand as a ‘military invasion’”, adding that South Korea’s claims were a “farce to evade the responsibility for the ever-escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula”.

North Korea’s ongoing border fortification efforts were “a legitimate and just exercise of its sovereignty going in strict conformity with the UN Charter”, the letter states, while also criticising South Korea for violating the charter by firing warning shots at soldiers in the DMZ.

South Korea has said it fires shots to make North Korean soldiers return to the north when they cross the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) that runs through the DMZ. In recent years, North Korean personnel have been building tactical roads and fences near the MDL.

The South Korean Unification Ministry said on Monday that Pyongyang’s letter aims to “justify its border fortification work” and serve as a “countermeasure” to Seoul’s message to the UN, the Yonhap news agency reported.

Last week, South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs sent a letter to the president of the UNSC, casting blame on North Korea for the landmine blast and calling it a “clear violation of the armistice agreement”.

The United States-led UN Command also said mine placement by North Korea violated the Armistice Agreement, signed in 1953 to end hostilities in the Korean War.

Days before North Korea’s letter to the UN, South ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Korea’s ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Defence Ministry proposed military talks to Pyongyang to “mutually confirm the precise location” of their border to reduce the risk of accidental clashes.
