articles.title: Brazil election results 2026: Key takeaways from Lula’s historic win
articles.summary: Lula wins a fourth term after a dramatic run-off marred by voting confusion and allegations of interference.
articles.body:
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has pulled off a political comeback that no Brazilian presidential candidate has managed in nearly four decades.

On Sunday, the 80-year-old leftist president won a record fourth non-consecutive term, overcoming a first-round defeat to right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Lula won more than 51 percent of the vote to Bolsonaro’s 48 percent. Some 98.76 percent of the ballots were counted when electoral authorities declared him the winner.

Sunday’s results were far from certain, keeping Brazilians on edge until the very end. Bolsonaro and Lula had been virtually tied in the polls in the lead-up to the election.

A last-minute decision to extend voting hours sparked accusations of election interference and questions about whether the result could face legal challenges.

Already, Senator Bolsonaro has pledged to annul the vote, crediting the extended hours with sowing voter confusion.

Lula makes history with an unprecedented re-election

Just three weeks ago, Lula looked like he was in trouble.

Bolsonaro had surprised many observers by beating the incumbent in the first round of voting on October 4, winning 47.03 percent of the vote to Lula’s 45.16 percent. The difference was 2.2 million votes.

But Lula spent the next three weeks trying to bring back voters who stayed home in the first round, while making a renewed pitch to those concerned about the cost of living and the future of his signature social programmes.

In the final days of the campaign, opinion polls showed the two candidates virtually tied.

Bolsonaro briefly took the lead as ballots were counted on Sunday evening. But Lula ultimately pulled ahead as results began arriving from the northeast, according to the Reuters news agency.

The northeast has long been a strong source of support for Lula and his Workers’ Party.

Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has large bases of support in the south and southeast of the country, as well as the centre-west.

For Lula, the victory means an unprecedented fourth term as president. For Bolsonaro, Sunday marks a defeat in his bid to return his family to the presidency.

No other candidate in modern Brazilian history has placed second in the first round of a presidential vote only to win in a run-off.

At age 80, Lula is also on track to beat his own record as the oldest Brazilian president to be sworn in since the country’s return to democracy.

Brazil’s last-minute voting extension sparks confusion

As the presidential run-off entered its final hours on Sunday, both campaigns were calling for voting to be extended.

Lula’s campaign accused local officials of deliberately reducing public transport services in several cities, making it difficult for lower-income voters to reach polling stations.

Bolsonaro’s campaign, meanwhile, requested more time for voters in areas affected by heavy rain and flooding.

In Minas Gerais, the regional electoral court reported that 349 polling locations had lost electricity, although voting machines continued operating on backup batteries, according to local media.

Originally, voting was scheduled to end at 5pm Brasilia time (20:00 GMT).

But faced with the two campaigns’ petitions for an extension, Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ordered polling stations to remain open for another two hours, until 7pm (22:00 GMT).

The decision, however, came after some stations had already closed and shut down their electronic voting machines.

Zanin later clarified that polling stations that had already closed would remain shut. Only those that were still open could continue accepting voters until 7pm.

The result was confusion over who could still vote, with some Brazilians turned away despite the extension.

In a brief post-election address, Bolsonaro pointed to those issues as a reason to annul the vote. He also accused Zanin of judicial malfeasance.

“He changes the rules of the game mid-game,” Bolsonaro said.

Election interference allegations raise prospect of legal challenges

Brazil’s Federal Police are investigating alleged election-related transport disruptions in five states.

In Salvador, a court ordered the arrest of the city’s transport secretary over allegations he had directed cuts to bus services. Lula’s camp pointed to such incidents as evidence of election interference.

Bolsonaro levelled similar allegations against Zanin, pointing to his history as Lula’s personal lawyer. Lula named Zanin to the Supreme Court in 2023.

“It is impossible to recognise the results of the election,” Bolsonaro told his supporters, calling the circumstances “unacceptable”.

He is likely to pursue a court challenge in an effort to overturn his defeat. Already, some figures on the global right have signalled their support.

Donald Trump Jr, the son of United States President Donald Trump, voiced outrage over the decision to extend the voting hours.

“If a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they’re just choosing to be silent because it’s all for the cause,” Trump Jr posted on social media.

The Trump administration has backed the Bolsonaro family, echoing its claims that Jair Bolsonaro, the former president, was subject to a political “witch-hunt” in the courts.

Flavio Bolsonaro has called for reforming Brazil’s courts in the aftermath of his father’s legal troubles. Earlier this month, Bolsonaro said that if he were elected, he would seek changes to Brazil’s Constitution to “re-democratise” the country.

Al Jazeera correspondent Monica Yanakiew signalled that the tensions between Brazil’s right wing and its court system are likely to re-emerge after Sunday’s election results.

“The judicial system itself is very divided,” Yanakiew said, pointing to rifts within the Supreme Court. “There will need to be a lot of political negotiation.”

Higher-than-expected turnout may have helped Lula win, according to Andrei Roman, the head of polling firm AtlasIntel, who cited a drop in voter abstention as one factor behind the president’s victory.

An estimated 33.4 million Brazilians stayed home during the October 4 first round, despite voting being compulsory for most adults. That amounted to about 21 percent of the electorate, the highest abstention rate in a general election since 1998.

The question now is how much of a difference those voters made. With more than 2.2 million votes separating the candidates in the first round, even a relatively small change in turnout could have mattered in the run-off.

The final turnout figures, particularly in each candidate’s strongholds, could help explain how Lula managed to turn the race around.

Lula also made last-ditch pitches in the final weeks of his campaign, designed to energise his working-class base. Among them was a promise to pursue free public transport on weekends.

Lula’s victory complicates Trump’s ambitions in Latin America

Lula’s victory comes amid a wave of right-wing electoral wins across Latin America, where Trump has sought to expand Washington’s influence.

The Bolsonaro family has long enjoyed Trump’s support. Reuters reported on Saturday that officials in Trump’s State Department had pushed for sanctions against Brazil as part of an effort to weaken Lula and return the Bolsonaro family to power.

Asked on Sunday whom he wanted to win, the US president would not name a candidate.

“I don’t want to get into that, but we are watching,” he told reporters.

Though Trump has been vocal in his support for other right-wing candidates in Latin America, he was relatively circumspect with regard to the Brazilian election, something critics have speculated was intentional.

While Bolsonaro has promised closer ties with the US, Lula made defending Brazil’s sovereignty and resisting foreign interference a central theme of his campaign.

He has often pointed to Trump’s aggressive tariff campaign and his public statements about the Jair Bolsonaro trial as evidence of foreign interference. Lula’s campaign has also clashed with US-based social media companies, prompting Trump to accuse his government of censorship.

In his victory speech, Lula described having to “overcome interference coming from the outside” in his bid for a fourth term.

“The election was a defeat for denialism,” Lula said on Sunday night. “It was a defeat for lies.”

He finished his speech by praising his “army” of supporters.

“I highly doubt that Russia, China, or the United States possess an army as victorious as the army of democracy in this country,” Lula said, thanking the voters.

articles.title: Forty Iranian sailors stranded off Sri Lanka coast rescued
articles.summary: The sailors received medical treatment before being flown back to Iran, Sri Lankan authorities said.
articles.body:
Sri Lanka's foreign ministry says it has coordinated efforts to treat and repatriate 40 Iranian sailors suffering from unspecified medical emergencies in international waters off the island's southeastern coast.

Ministry spokesperson Thushara Rodrigo told BBC Sinhala they received a distress call on Saturday from Iranian ships "regarding an urgent medical need".

The rescue operation was planned by the Iranian Embassy in Colombo, he said.

Iranian ships have been stranded at sea due to a US naval blockade. Sri Lanka stresses it is neutral in the conflict, but has at times offered help to Iranian sailors in what it says is an obligation to international law.

A BBC Sinhala report last month found that there were 21 Iranian vessels located in international waters near Sri Lanka.

The 40 rescued sailors served on different ships - though Sri Lankan authorities do not have information on how many ships they belonged to, Rodrigo said.

The sailors were brought ashore and taken to Colombo for medical treatment before being sent back to Iran by plane on Saturday night, he added.

He said that several agencies were involved in the operation, including local shipping companies.

According to Rodrigo, Sri Lanka was obliged under international law and humanitarian grounds to provide the necessary facilities for medical emergencies.

"This does not mean that we will provide assistance to those ships," he said. "It is generally an internationally accepted tradition to respond to a distress call after receiving it."

"We have dealt with such cases before. This is a normal process that continues to be implemented."

The ongoing conflict in Iran started when the US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on the country in February. Iran responded by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a critical international trade route.

Attacks by both sides have persisted as negotiations stalled.

Sri Lanka has sought to remain neutral in the conflict, having rejected military access requests from both the US and Iran and urged both parties to prioritise dialogue.

It has also offered assistance to Iranian ships caught in the conflict on what it argues are humanitarian grounds.

In March, Sri Lankan authorities said they responded to a distress call from the Iranian ship the Iris Dena, which had sunk off its coast after a US torpedo attack.

More than 80 crew members were killed in the attack, and injured survivors were taken to a hospital near the Galle Harbour.

The following day, Sri Lankan authorities allowed another Iranian naval vessel to dock at one of its ports, with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake saying that they would "never hesitate to protect humanity".

Sri Lankan authorities said earlier this month they had no immediate plans to send aid to 19 Iranian ships near its coasts which had reported shortages of food, water and fuel. The authorities said they had to prioritise national interests, the Associated Press reported.

articles.title: World reacts to Lula’s victory in Brazil’s presidential election
articles.summary: International leaders and politicians congratulate the Brazilian president on his re-election.
articles.body:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has secured a fourth nonconsecutive term, defeating right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in a run-off .

Bolsonaro, however, has called for Sunday’s vote to be annulled over an “unacceptable” two-hour voting extension granted by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin despite both candidates having requested additional voting time.

The election results have drawn reactions across the world, with left-wing global figures celebrating Lula’s victory.

Sheinbaum congratulated Lula in a post on X. “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won,” she wrote.

In his congratulatory post, Carney credited Lula with advancing relations between Canada and Brazil.

“Let us seize this opportunity to strengthen them further, together – to create new promising commercial prospects, protect the environment, and ensure greater prosperity for both our populations,” he wrote on X.

US President Donald Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr criticised the result, citing the two-hour voting time extension.

“If a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they’re just choosing to be silent because it’s all for the cause,” he said.

Progressive Senator Bernie Sanders, meanwhile, congratulated Lula’s “extraordinary re-election victory”, saying the Brazilian president has “stood up” for workers and democracy and will continue to do so for the next four years.

Congressman Ro Khanna said in a post on X: “People all across the world are fighting back against extremism. With Lula in Brazil, they just won. Authoritarian leaders always attack democracy because they stand no chance against the will of their people.”

Khanna added that Trump “must respect the results and not undermine Brazil’s elections”.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote on X: “The people united will never be defeated!”

California Governor Gavin Newsom’s media office released a statement, saying he is “proud to stand with Brazil and partners around the world who share our commitment to defending democracy, protecting our environment, strengthening workers’ rights, and building an economy that works for working families”.

Diaz-Canel said Lula’s “historic” win “ensures the continuity of the path of peace, sovereignty, and social justice embarked upon by the Brazilian people under your leader”.

“Brazil can count on Cuba in the construction of the unity and integration of our Great Homeland, Latin American and Caribbean,” he wrote in a post on X.

Kast said he spoke on the phone with Lula to congratulate him on his victory.

“Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead, and we will continue working on an agenda that strengthens relations between our countries in economic integration and the fight against organised crime in the region,” he said on X.

In a congratulatory post on X, Fujimori reaffirmed Peru’s “willingness to strengthen our strategic alliance, integration, cooperation and the sustainable development of the Amazon that we share” with Brazil.

“Bolivia and Brazil are neighbouring and sister countries, united by a shared history and common challenges,” Rodrigo wrote on X.

The two countries will continue to work together to strengthen ties and “generate more opportunities for our nations”, he added.

“I congratulate the ‌‌‌‌Brazilian ‌‌‌‌people for this democratic day and especially President Lula for the victory!” Mulino wrote on X. “We will continue working together for our countries.”

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen

Von der Leyen congratulated Lula on X, proclaiming that democracy and multilateralism “have won” in Brazil.

“Europe’s partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come,” she added. “Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate.”

“Our region has common enemies, shared challenges, and much to gain when we work together,” Noboa wrote on X, congratulating Lula.

“I salute the Brazilian people for this great democratic journey,” Pena wrote on X.

“Paraguay and Brazil share a common agenda of integration and development. We will continue working together for the wellbeing of our people.”

Orsi wrote on X that he had just spoken with his “friend” Lula and congratulated him “on the victory and on the democratic celebration that an electoral process represents”.

Argentina’s former President Cristina Kirchner

“Congratulations,” Kirchner wrote on X, “first to the Brazilian people”, and also to Lula, for knowing “how to awaken in your compatriots feeling and sense to win this battle”.

articles.title: Australian murderer loses bid to eat Vegemite in prison
articles.summary: Andre McKechnie, who murdered a property developer, argued it was his right to enjoy Australian culture.
articles.body:
A convicted murderer serving a life sentence in Australia has lost his bid to overturn a ban on prisoners consuming Vegemite - the salty yeast-based spread that has become a national symbol.

Andre McKechnie argued that the ban, in place since 2006, denied him the right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian".

Authorities in the state of Victoria say inmates may use the strong-smelling paste to disguise contraband substances or to brew alcohol behind bars.

And on Monday, a Supreme Court judge rejected McKechnie's appeal, saying the prisoner's "cultural rights are limited primarily by the fact he has been sentenced to a term of imprisonment".

In his lawsuit against Victoria's Department of Justice and Corrections, the agency which manages the state's prisons, McKechnie, 54, said the ban on the spread breached law requiring prisons to provide food that allowed inmates to maintain their health and well-being but the judge said that had not been proven.

McKechnie was handed a life sentence for stabbing a property developer to death in Queensland in the 1990s. He served part of his sentence in Queensland before being transferred to Victoria.

During the hearing, the court heard evidence from Corrections Victoria that the smell of vegemite can distract sniffer dogs trying to detect drugs being brought into prison.

The product is also banned in jails in Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania.

A much-loved breakfast spread for some, Vegemite has acquired controversial accolades since it first hit shop shelves in Australia in 1923.

The thick, brown spread was invented in the Victorian capital of Melbourne more than a century ago as an alternative to the British spread Marmite.

It sparked an international dispute in April last year when an Australian cafe owner in Canada was told to remove jars of the condiment from his shelves as it did not comply with local health regulations.

Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese intervened in the row, saying it was "rather odd" that Canada allowed the sale of Vegemite's "rubbish" rival product Marmite. The cafe owner was later allowed to continue selling the spread.

articles.title: US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls
articles.summary: Judge questions Trump-led effort to exert greater influence over the electoral process ahead of upcoming midterm vote.
articles.body:
A United States appeals court has expressed doubt over the Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California, which seeks to force the state to throw out mail-in ballots it has deemed likely to go to noncitizens.

Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said on Sunday the three-judge panel would issue a decision as soon as possible, following a rare weekend oral argument.

But Bennett, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump, voiced concern that the lawsuit would not hold up to scrutiny.

He pointed to the Elections Clause in the US Constitution, which allows states — not the federal government — to administer elections.

“It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause,” Bennett told Justice Department lawyer Matthew Donnelly. “How can we do that?”

The case is part of a larger effort under the right-wing Trump administration to crack down on alleged noncitizen voting ahead of the crucial November 3 midterm elections.

On October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm races, the Justice Department issued a complaint targeting California, a left-wing stronghold.

It asked the federal court system to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots that the government says were sent to “likely noncitizens”.

The lawsuit indicates the Trump administration sent California officials a list of 20,000 names it believes are not eligible to vote, based on citizenship.

Trump has often pushed the discredited claim that the Democratic Party is benefitting from widespread voting by noncitizens.

California has long been one of the targets of his election misinformation.

Earlier this year, Trump denounced the state’s primaries after right-wing candidates like Los Angeles mayoral hopeful Spencer Pratt felt short of his expectations.

“There’s BIG cheating by the Dumocrats in California,” he wrote on social media at the time.

He then announced that the state would be under investigation by the US Attorneys’ Office.

Trump’s efforts have caused alarm, with critics accusing him of seeking to dampen voter turnout through intimidation and confusion.

The midterms will decide which party controls the US Congress, as well as key state and local positions.

Polls, however, predict steep odds for Republican candidates, given Trump’s souring approval ratings and dissatisfaction with issues like the cost of living and the US-Israel war on Iran.

Voting rights advocates have warned that the Trump administration has not publicly revealed how it has compiled its list of noncitizen voters, and whistleblower reports have cast doubt on the accuracy of such lists.

In response to the October 15 lawsuit, California has countered that it has strong safeguards to prevent noncitizens from voting.

It also said the Justice Department’s claims are based on dubious data.

“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day,” California Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement earlier this month.

“We will continue to carry out free and fair elections in the Golden State — and call out this authoritarian as he tries every play in the dictator’s playbook.”

articles.title: The Gambia’s first blind magistrate tests a system built for the sighted
articles.summary: For a decade, Muhammed Krubally has shown what is possible and what still needs to change.
articles.body:
Banjul, the Gambia – It is still early when Magistrate Muhammed Krubally arrives at the Banjul Magistrates’ Court.

Before the first case, his clerk goes over the day’s proceedings, running through the files and making sure everything is in place. Krubally listens, asks questions, and prepares to preside.

Then he enters a packed courtroom, where lawyers, witnesses and relatives have gathered for a criminal case.

Krubally cannot see the people before him, but he can hear them. A lawyer rises. A witness speaks. Papers move across the room. His clerk is nearby.

At his desk, his computer speaks back to him.

Krubally uses JAWS, or Job Access With Speech, a screen reader that allows him to navigate his computer and read documents and judgements.

“This makes my job very easy,” he tells Al Jazeera.

He also uses AI-enabled smart glasses to access information and carry out tasks independently.

But technology is only part of how he works.

He listens for voices, remembers details and follows the rhythm of proceedings, building a picture of the courtroom through sound. When necessary, he relies on his clerk.

At 41, Krubally says he has presided over more than 1,000 civil and criminal cases since joining the bench.

In 2016, he became the Gambia’s first visually impaired magistrate. The Gambia Organisation of the Visually Impaired (GOVI) identifies him as the country’s first person with a visual impairment to hold the position.

For Krubally, this is not an experiment in what a visually impaired person might be capable of doing.

Long before he took his place on the bench, Krubally grew up in a village in the Gambia’s Central River Region, the second of nine children.

From an early age, he wanted to become a lawyer. Part of that ambition was personal: he wanted to defend his own rights. But he also wanted to advocate for others.

He wanted, he says, “to be the voice for the voiceless”, particularly people with disabilities.

From primary school through university, Krubally encountered limited resources and an education system that often left visually impaired students like him facing obstacles their sighted classmates did not.

He remembers being discouraged by fellow students and some teachers from pursuing the education he wanted.

Instead of making him abandon his ambition, he says, their doubts only strengthened it.

“Their discouragement kept me going. I knew what I wanted, and see where I am now,” he says.

Those experiences later shaped his decision to enter the judiciary.

“I became a magistrate to change the system, to make it inclusive,” he says.

But joining one of the country’s most important public institutions did not make those barriers disappear.

The Gambia’s Persons with Disabilities Act, passed in 2021, sets out principles including independence, non-discrimination, full participation, equality of opportunity and accessibility.

The law also contains provisions covering employment, public buildings and services, information and access to justice.

Yet putting those rights into practice remains a challenge.

The National Human Rights Commission has identified barriers affecting people with disabilities, including discrimination and difficulties accessing services, education and employment.

Al Jazeera contacted the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Welfare for a response on implementation of the act, including measures to improve accessibility, education and employment opportunities for people with disabilities. The ministry did not respond.

Krubally encounters those challenges not only as a judicial officer, but also as an advocate.

As president of the Gambia Federation of the Disabled, he speaks at events in the Gambia and beyond, pressing for greater recognition of the rights and potential of people with disabilities.

“I want to see a world for all; inclusion matters,” he says.

For Krubally, inclusion is not simply about opening the door. It is about having the means to participate once inside.

For many people with disabilities, working towards full inclusion begins long before they enter a courtroom or parliament.

Today, GOVI’s Resource Centre for the Blind provides specialist education for children with visual impairments before they transition into mainstream schools.

Forty-nine pupils aged between four and 14 currently attend the centre, Lamin Colley, its head of school, told Al Jazeera.

After completing their studies there, pupils are expected to enter mainstream schools, where special-needs teachers stationed across school clusters are meant to support them.

Colley told Al Jazeera that limited learning materials and the size of the school clusters are putting pressure on the support available to students. A single special-needs teacher, he said, cannot maintain regular contact with all students across those clusters.

“The reality on the ground is that not much has changed after the disability act has been passed,” Colley says.

He attributes this partly to what he describes as insufficient government funding for disability issues in the national budget.

Colley remembers Krubally as a pupil who loved to read and could often be found in the library. He also remembers his determination to participate in activities alongside his sighted classmates.

Years later, Krubally’s journey carries a message beyond the school gates.

But one person’s achievement does not erase the obstacles facing those coming behind him.

Ndey Yassin Secka-Sallah knows what it means to enter a public institution without having the tools to participate independently.

She was nominated to the Gambia’s National Assembly and has long advocated for the rights of people with disabilities. GOVI describes her as the country’s only visually impaired parliamentarian.

She was also involved in advocacy around disability rights and the push for stronger legal protections.

Yet taking a seat in parliament did not make the institution accessible.

“I used to depend on my fellow colleagues to know what was being discussed,” she told Al Jazeera.

What she wanted was not special treatment, but independence.

“I would have loved to be independent, without depending on people for help.”

Five years after the disability law was passed, Secka-Sallah says implementation remains a major challenge.

She sees Krubally’s appointment to the bench as significant, but not as the end of the struggle.

“Inclusion is all we wish for,” she says.

Musa Barrow, another visually impaired professional, teaches media law and ethics to journalism students.

Like Krubally, Barrow has encountered assumptions about what a visually impaired person can do. Some students have questioned whether he can meet the standards they expect from a lecturer.

Technology has helped him work independently. He uses digital tools to read, write and prepare lecture notes.

“Technology has broken that barrier for me,” he says.

But students’ assumptions have not disappeared.

“I can do more than what sighted people can do,” he says.

Barrow’s visual impairment has also shaped how he teaches journalism, particularly when discussing the media’s portrayal of disability.

The experiences of Krubally, Secka-Sallah and Barrow all point to the same gap: entering an institution is not the same as being equipped to participate fully in it.

What does the law look like in practice?

The scale of the challenge is difficult to measure.

The Gambia’s 2013 Population and Housing Census recorded a disability prevalence of 1.2 percent, representing 21,873 people, according to later analysis of the census data.

But that figure may understate the scale of disability in the country. The census used a narrower set of questions and did not use the Washington Group questions commonly used to measure functional difficulties.

The Gambia has since conducted a new population and housing census, with preliminary results released in September 2024. But the preliminary report did not include detailed updated national disability data.

That leaves an incomplete picture of how the country’s disability landscape may have changed over the past decade.

What is clearer is the experience of people navigating institutions that were not designed with them in mind: a parliamentarian depending on colleagues to follow proceedings, a lecturer being questioned about his ability to teach, or children entering mainstream schools with limited specialist support.

He now mentors young people, many of them visually impaired. One is Modou Lamin Dampha, who describes Krubally as someone who encourages him to keep pursuing his ambitions.

“He advises and encourages me to keep going, that things are possible,” Dampha says.

For Dampha, Krubally is more than a magistrate.

He is evidence that professional ambition does not have to end with disability.

Back inside the Banjul Magistrates’ Court, the case continues.

Krubally listens as the proceedings unfold, using voices, memory, technology and experience to follow what is happening before him.

His career raises a harder question: how much has the system itself changed?

The judiciary was asked what accommodations are available to Krubally, what accessibility measures are in place for judicial officers and court users with disabilities, and what changes it has made since the Persons with Disabilities Act was passed.

It did not respond by the time of publication.

Krubally has spent a decade adapting to the demands of the courtroom.

Whether the institution around him has also adapted remains an open question.

Asked what he sees when he looks to the future, Krubally says it is not about the obstacles he has overcome.

articles.title: Leafy spurge may have arrived in North America through a Massachusetts ballast dump in 1827; contaminated crop seeds later helped the invasive plant spread across the US and Canada
articles.summary: A plant native to Eurasia was recorded in North America in 1827, likely introduced through a ballast dump in Massachusetts.
articles.body: A plant native to Eurasia was recorded in North America in 1827, likely introduced through a ballast dump in Massachusetts. Known as leafy spurge (Euphorbia esula), the species later spread across the northern United States and southern Canada.According to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), several introductions may have occurred, while contaminated crop seeds helped the plant establish in new areas. By the early 1900s, leafy spurge was widespread across the region. It is an invasive, non-native plant and is particularly common in parts of the Great Plains and the western United States. Its extensive root system and ability to reproduce from both seeds and roots help it persist and spread in a range of habitats over time.How leafy spurge first arrived in North AmericaThe first US collection of leafy spurge was made in 1827 in Newbury, Massachusetts. The plant was thought to have originated from a ballast dump, although the review says there were likely multiple introductions into North America. A review cited by the Forest Service suggests at least four possible early introductions.The first Canadian collection was recorded in 1899 in Huron County, Ontario. The species was brought by Russian immigrants in contaminated spelt from Germany. Early spread was also linked to the planting and cultivation of contaminated smooth brome and cereal seed originating both inside and outside North America. These records point to several possible routes by which the plant became established across the continent over time.Leafy spurge became widespread across North America by the early 1900sBy the early 1900s, leafy spurge was widespread in the northern United States and southern Canada. It had been recorded in Ontario by 1889 and Iowa by 1899. Around 1900, it was described as naturalised in parts of the northeastern United States, while reports also placed it in Oregon and Washington.It was recorded in Idaho in the early 1900s. The Forest Service identifies Oregon, Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Minnesota, and Wisconsin among the states where leafy spurge is most widespread and invasive. In western Canada, it occurs as far north as Yukon. It is less common at the edges of its overall North American range and is rare along the Atlantic Coast.How did leafy spurge spread through roots and seedsLeafy spurge is an erect perennial plant that usually grows between 20 and 90 centimetres tall. Its narrow leaves grow along the stems, while leaves near the flower clusters are heart-shaped. When the stems are damaged, they release a milky fluid. The plant produces small seed capsules that split explosively when mature, ejecting seeds.It also regenerates from its root crown, root buds, and root fragments. Its persistent root system can be deep and extensive, allowing shoots to emerge even after above-ground growth has been damaged. The species grows in roadsides, old fields, pastures, meadows, areas beside rivers, and open woodlands. It can establish in disturbed sites and persist in many habitats.How did leafy spurge affect native plants and grazing animalsThe Forest Service describes leafy spurge as a highly invasive plant that can establish in stable, undisturbed native plant communities. Its rapid vegetative spread and dense stands can replace native or rare plants. Thick layers of plant litter may prevent light-demanding species from establishing, while other research discussed in the review suggests that the plant may also affect neighbouring vegetation through chemicals and changes to soil conditions.Leafy spurge is avoided by cattle and horses when other forage is available, and its milky sap can cause severe diarrhoea in both animals. Control is difficult because roots can survive after above-ground growth is removed. Sheep, goats and introduced insects, including flea beetles, have been used to reduce its abundance.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1982, a Minnesota farmer wrote a will leaving his 300-acre farm to his son after his wife's lifetime; a different 1989 will later emerged, and a 2026 appeals court reversed the reopening of his estate
articles.summary: A Minnesota inheritance dispute over a 300-acre farm has taken another turn after an appeals court reversed a lower court's decision to reopen a deceased
articles.body: A Minnesota inheritance dispute over a 300-acre farm has taken another turn after an appeals court reversed a lower court's decision to reopen a deceased farmer's estate, years after a second will surfaced. In a September 8, 2026, ruling, the Minnesota Court of Appeals held that a court's failure to meet a statutory requirement for medical-assistance claims clearance did not deprive it of the authority to decide the estate case. The decision restored the legal standing of a 2017 property decree that had been set aside, according to the court's published opinion in In re the Estate of Clarence Vatthauer.The case centres on two wills signed by Clarence Vatthauer, who owned and farmed approximately 300 acres of productive farmland and cattle pasture in Red Lake County, Minnesota. His 1982 will gave his wife, Fern Vatthauer, the right to use the property during her lifetime, with the remainder passing to their son, David Vatthauer. A second will, executed in 1989, revoked the earlier document and left the land to Fern outright. The competing documents eventually triggered a family dispute over who was entitled to inherit the property.A second will emerges years after the farmer's deathClarence died in 2005. In 2015, David petitioned the district court to distribute his father's estate and submitted the 1982 will. The court issued a decree of descent in 2017, establishing property ownership according to that document. At the time, the record did not indicate that any family member knew about the later will. David had also not filed a clearance for medical-assistance claims against his father's estate, a statutory requirement for a court to issue a decree of descent.The dispute resurfaced after Clarence's daughter, Julie Ford, was appointed guardian of Fern in 2022 as her health declined. Ford contacted the law firm that had handled her parents' estate planning and discovered the 1989 wills executed by both Clarence and Fern. Clarence's later will changed the inheritance arrangement substantially. Instead of giving Fern a lifetime interest followed by ownership passing to David, it gave her the farm outright. Fern's own 1989 will directed that her property be distributed equally among her children.Ford sought to have the earlier decree vacated and Clarence's 1989 will admitted to probate. She argued that the 2017 decree was void because the court had issued it without the required clearance for medical-assistance claims. She also argued that exceptional circumstances justified reopening the case.Fern died in October 2023. The district court subsequently ordered the two 1989 wills probated, vacated the 2017 decree and ruled that the farm had passed to Fern outright before being distributed equally among her surviving children under her will.Why the appeals court reversed the decisionDavid challenged the lower court's decision, arguing that the failure to obtain the clearance did not strip the court of subject-matter jurisdiction, or its legal authority to hear and decide the type of case involved. The Minnesota Court of Appeals agreed with him. In its September 2026 opinion, the court acknowledged that the district court had violated the statutory requirement. However, it drew a distinction between making a legal or procedural error and lacking the jurisdiction to decide a case.Minnesota law grants district courts broad jurisdiction over matters relating to deceased people's estates. Although state law requires medical-assistance claims to be cleared or resolved before a decree of descent is entered, the appeals court found no clear legislative statement that violating this requirement removes a court's subject-matter jurisdiction.The judges therefore concluded that the 2017 decree was not automatically void simply because the required clearance had not been filed. The legal error could have been challenged through the appropriate correction or appeal procedures, but the ordinary appeal period had expired years before the lower court attempted to vacate the decree.The appeals court also rejected the argument that the case should be sent back for the district court to reconsider whether exceptional circumstances justified reopening it. It said the relevant procedural rule did not provide a mechanism for correcting the type of judicial error involved.Finality of inheritance decisions at stakeThe ruling highlights a broader legal principle: courts must balance the need to correct mistakes against the need for finality in inheritance proceedings. The appeals court noted that allowing a final estate decree to be challenged years later on the basis of a legal error could leave property ownership uncertain long after an estate had been distributed.The judges referred to Minnesota's probate code, which aims to provide an efficient process for settling estates and distributing property to successors. They also cited established precedent emphasising that parties generally must use the prescribed appeal process to challenge a court's decision rather than reopen it indefinitely.The case was reversed and remanded, meaning it was sent back to the district court for further orders consistent with the appeals court's ruling. The lower court must recognise that it improperly vacated the 2017 decree and that the decree became final when no party appealed it within the required period.The decision does not mean the appeals court found that the 1982 will was necessarily the last valid will. Instead, it held that the lower court could not invalidate the earlier decree on the jurisdictional grounds it had relied upon.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: China’s political elite gather for talks on Communist Party discipline
articles.summary: The four-day meeting is being watched closely for clues as to the country’s direction and future leadership.
articles.body:
China’s political leaders and elites have begun a four-day meeting to discuss ways to strengthen discipline within the ruling Communist Party, as President Xi Jinping pushes for greater loyalty from officials and deepens his anticorruption campaign.

The fifth plenum, which started on Monday, is also being watched closely for clues to the country’s direction and future leadership.

The closed-door gathering comes roughly a year before Xi is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as party leader and ahead of expected personnel changes to key leadership bodies.

Roughly 300 members of the Communist Party’s Central Committee are attending.

While Xi has consolidated his grip on power, analysts say the plenum will give him another chance to align what Chinese officials do with what Beijing wants.

“The plenum is a chance to ensure the new generations rising [through] the ranks share Xi’s assessment of the opportunities and risks China faces,” Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London’s Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, told The Associated Press news agency.

“The plenum is a chance to ensure the new generations rising through the ranks share Xi’s assessment of the opportunities and risks China faces,” Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London’s Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, told The Associated Press news agency.

Previous plenums have helped Xi to cement his authority.

The Chinese leader has waged a 14-year campaign against corruption that has purged thousands of officials, including dozens of committee members.

Yet Xi remains frustrated with cadres he says are still not implementing his orders.

In a January speech, published by state media in advance of this week’s plenum, he railed against “two-faced” officials who appear to comply with directives but “inwardly resist”, are “politically opportunistic” and pursue “individualism”.

During the plenum, the committee will discuss a draft policy decision on advancing “full and rigorous party self-governance,” China’s official Xinhua news agency reported.

The push is meant to make cadres more disciplined, effective and less corrupt.

Analysts say Xi is trying to maximise efficiency and loyalty among cadres by imposing more supervision and rules.

Neil Thomas, senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said he expects demands for tighter scrutiny of public spending and major projects, more use of technology to uncover corruption and tougher consequences for officials who fail to deliver on Xi’s priorities.

Because of Xi’s extensive purges, this year’s plenum is expected to have the lowest turnout since former leader Mao Zedong died in 1976.

Eight of the Central Committee’s seats are vacant, with another 15 members under investigation and at risk of being replaced.

Xi’s anticorruption drive has also targeted the military , toppling five of the seven members of the Central Military Commission (CMC), the party’s top armed forces body.

The plenum could see new members appointed to the CMC, and Xi might even restructure the party’s control over the military.

The talks come as the world’s second-largest economy is struggling to address persistently sluggish domestic spending and a protracted crisis in the crucial property sector.

Turbulent political and economic ties with the United States are weighing on China’s leaders as well.

articles.title: Walking in Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru? Here’s what nobody tells you
articles.summary: Walking in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru is difficult because the footpaths are broken, blocked or non-existent, and road planning has always given priority
articles.body: Walking in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru is difficult because the footpaths are broken, blocked or non-existent, and road planning has always given priority to vehicles over people. Every city has its problem — the wide and fast roads, and heat in Delhi; the pavements doubling up as markets and parking in Mumbai; the construction and damaged slabs in Bengaluru.Poor lighting, no ramps, and pollution further push women, the elderly and the disabled away. As walking falls, traffic, pollution and health costs climb. The answer is continuous footpaths, safe crossings, legal vending spaces, shade and lighting, and treating pedestrians as primary road users instead of an afterthought.Footpath is there, butWalk down any major road in Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru, and you will see the same pattern: a pavement begins, then disappears. It may end at a tree, a transformer box, a metro pillar or a heap of construction debris. Planners record the kilometers of footpath constructed, but that number conceals how much of it is continuous, wide enough for two people to pass, and unobstructed. For a pedestrian a pavement that is not usable from end to end is hardly a pavement.Pedestrian is the last thing on everyone’s mindFor the last two decades Indian cities have been busy widening roads, building flyovers and creating signal-free corridors. The idea was to speed up vehicles and the space for it in many places was taken straight off the footpath. Pedestrians are rarely included in discussions about road budgets, but make up a significant portion of daily trips. Figures from Delhi and Mumbai consistently show that pedestrians are a large part of the road deaths. When those most at risk are the least prepared for, the result is predictable.Three cities, three separate problemsEach city fails walkers in its own unique way. The pain points in Delhi are wide, fast roads, long distances between crossing and summer heat that makes walking at midday punishing. In Mumbai pavements often are the only open space available and so they double up as markets, parking and storefronts.Monsoon flooding adds another hazard. In Bengaluru, rapid growth, ongoing Metro construction and a long-running problem with the quality of pavements mean walkers regularly step onto the road to avoid broken slabs and open drains. The reasons are different but the result is the same. People do not want to walk.Unseen wallsSome roadblocks never appear in infrastructure audits. Walking in the evening is uncomfortable, especially for women, who often plan routes based on perceived safety, rather than distance, due to low light levels. For the elderly, parents with prams and wheelchair users, a missing ramp or uneven kerb can turn a short trip into an ordeal. Walking is a health trade-off due to air pollution, especially in Delhi during winter months. These factors reduce the number of people who can use the city on foot in subtle ways.When walking stops, cities payWe walk less, and it’s not just an inconvenience. If people stop walking short distances and hop on to two-wheelers or autos, congestion goes up, parking problems increase and the air quality deteriorates – which in turn makes walking even less appealing. Local shops lose customers, public transport loses passengers because the last half-kilometre to a station feels unsafe and sedentary lifestyles add to a growing public health burden. The expense of unwalkable streets is paid by the entire city.What a walkable Indian city requiresThe fixes are well understood, if difficult to implement. Cities need uninterrupted and unobstructed footpaths of a minimum standard width, with frequent and well-timed crossings. The footpaths and livelihoods can co-exist. Vendors should be provided with designated, legal space and not be treated as encroachers. Street trees, covered drains and good lighting take care of comfort and safety at the same time. Most importantly, road budgets and design standards should be based on the premise that pedestrians are the primary users of a street, not an afterthought. Some cities have started pilot projects such as retrofitting for pedestrian friendliness and complete streets guidelines, but the real test will be scaling them up beyond a few showcase stretches.The bottom lineWhat no one tells you about walking in India’s biggest cities is that it is almost never the walker’s fault. It’s not that people have become lazy or temperamentally car-dependent and therefore walked less; the city has made walking difficult, uncomfortable and sometimes dangerous. articles.title: Photos show potholes on road near Wisbech days before fatal crash
articles.summary: The pictures, taken by council representatives, reveal the poor condition of the riverside road.
articles.body:
Newly released photographs show a road riddled with potholes just days before a speeding car struck one and plunged into a river, killing two teenagers.

A VW Polo driven by Declan Berry was travelling at about 90mph (145km/h) moments before it entered the River Nene on North Brink, near Wisbech, Cambridgeshire, on 17 March, killing him and one of his passengers.

Four days earlier, Cambridgeshire County Council had ordered repairs to 98 potholes along the road, with the work scheduled to start on 3 April.

The authority said repairs to that section of North Brink had been "scheduled in line with our normal maintenance processes and response times".

Photographs obtained by the BBC through the Freedom of Information Act show the road's condition when council officials visited.

The repairs were carried out on 20 March, while the road was closed following the fatal crash.

An inquest last month heard that three other passengers escaped from the car, but that 16-year-old Eden Bunn died from a head injury.

The body of Berry, who was 18, was recovered from the river two weeks later.

One of the passengers told the hearing he had asked Berry to "slow down", but the driver replied: "We will be fine."

The speed limit on that stretch of North Brink is 60mph (96km/h).

A police report found the driver's speed was "the most significant contributory factor" to the crash, but that the condition of the road and presence of potholes also played a role.

The court heard the council had received 127 complaints about the road's condition in the months before the crash, including reports of potholes, mud and debris on the carriageway.

It is not known whether the pothole struck by Berry's car was among those photographed.

A council spokesperson said: "Our thoughts and sympathies remain with the families and friends of Declan Berry and Eden Bunn and all of those affected.

"We are aware of the coroner's findings that the condition of the road more than minimally contributed to the collision.

"Safety is our primary concern. We carefully prioritise our maintenance resources across the 4,500km of our road network.

"The most urgent defects are made safe within two hours and fully repaired within five days."

articles.title: The French government is hiding behind a ‘riots’ narrative
articles.summary: It is much easier to fearmonger and try to delegitimise the protests than to address students’ demands.
articles.body:
Images from the violent unrest in France have travelled around the world. Smashed shop windows, destroyed property, acts of looting and raging fires have rightly caused outrage and condemnation.

There is no single explanation of the motives of the perpetrators. There are certainly opportunistic “criminal elements” who take advantage of such situations. But there is also a lot of public anger that has boiled over after it had simmered for years as living conditions have deteriorated and demands for changes have been left unanswered.

The French government has taken full advantage of these violent acts, using them to justify the overly securitised response to the protests and to avoid public scrutiny for the failure to address its own failures. The images of chaos allow those in power to pose as the defenders of a public order they have actively helped undermine.

These acts of violence, however, cannot delegitimise the reasons behind the mass mobilisation of students across France. They also must not distract from the brutal police violence that has unfolded.

Fourteen-year-old Eden suffered a fractured jaw and had teeth knocked out by a tear gas grenade fired from a police launcher. Sixteen-year-old Mael lost the sight in one eye after a suspected hit from a police rubber bullet. Fifteen-year-old Evan had a hand blown off by a police stun grenade.

By October 14, 7,950 people had been placed in police custody since the protests began in September, 85 percent of them minors. A further 2,700 were taken into custody following the October 17 protests. Yesterday, police made another 1,000 arrests.

The staggering scale of detention and the mobilisation of tens of thousands of police officers make this one of the most heavily repressed protest movements of this century.

But there is also the quieter violence of social deprivation that the students are protesting and that has largely been ignored in the public narrative.

Across France, the sense of growing impoverishment deepens year after year. Poverty rates are the highest they have been since the 1990s, with 9.8 million people living under the official poverty line. Meanwhile, 53 French billionaires own as much wealth as nearly half of the French population, according to Oxfam.

Deteriorating socioeconomic conditions have hit the French educational system hard.

In Acoua, on the island of Mayotte, the Cite du Nord secondary school was blockaded as early as August 31. Long before protests in the Paris region attracted attention, parents and staff came out in protest to demand better learning and teaching conditions.

Built for 900 pupils, this school accommodates 2,300 in cramped, poorly ventilated classrooms. Alongside staff shortages, the school also struggles with water supply failures and unsanitary conditions in toilets.

In Sevran, a suburb of Paris, pupils and teachers at Blaise-Cendrars secondary school have complained since 2024 about water leaks, mould, unusable toilets, and shortages of tables and chairs.

At Marcelin-Berthelot secondary school in Pantin, another Parisian suburb, windows no longer open at a time when heatwaves can bring temperatures as high as 40C.

At Politzer secondary school in Bagnolet, also a Parisian suburb, staff, pupils and parents learnt in late September that the water was unsafe to drink, although it had been tested in June.

These are just a few examples of a countrywide trend of an educational infrastructure that is fast deteriorating, especially in impoverished areas.

This is compounded by the erosion of the level of education pupils actually receive. According to the education ministry’s own figures, 20.2 million teaching hours were not delivered in state secondary schools in 2024–25, excluding Mayotte: almost one in 10 scheduled hours. Of these, 15 million were lost because absent teachers were not replaced.

According to French economist Lucas Chancel, since 2017, when Emmanuel Macron came to power, government spending per student has declined by 20 percent.

This is the structural violence French students are asking those in power to end. Instead of listening, the government has responded with repressive tactics and narrative spin.

In his address to the public, Macron said he understood the students, but he did not express support for them the way he did for police officers. A meeting with 20 students on Friday resulted in a promise to reform the university entrance platform – not to address the students’ key demands.

Macron has doubled down on the security “solution”, deploying 70,000 police officers and pledging to ban protests. He has accused the “far left” of seeking to “bring down the republic”.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has called on the left to “choose a side”: the Republic equated with the police, or the rioters and their “violent agenda”. As if taking part in a protest amounted to an attack on the state.

Unsurprisingly, the far right is revelling in the chaos that appears to be engulfing the country, obscuring these needs by focusing on the presumed origins of people filmed committing acts of violence. Some far-right politicians have denounced the “hordes of thugs of foreign origin”, others have called for broader powers to strip people of their citizenship.

This rhetoric serves Macron’s political camp well as it allows it to present itself once again as the last defence against the far right, asking the general population to rally behind out of fear rather than because of its governance record. Voters are offered an increasingly bleak choice between those who have fuelled their anger and those seeking to turn it into racial hatred.

At this point, it is clear the government does not seem interested in genuinely addressing the demands of the students is in the cards. Doing so would mean confronting the priorities of Macron’s presidency: protecting the wealth of the few and abandoning the many.

Instead, the government will wait for the movement to exhaust itself, be weakened by fear or be discredited by unrest, until it dies out on its own.

This strategy, however, is a failed one. Even if this protest movement fizzles out, a new one will soon replace it. The French people cannot be scared into complacency forever while their living conditions continue to deteriorate.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: 'Lula would strengthen Brazil’s commitment to multipolarity': Shashi Tharoor
articles.summary: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor has welcomed Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election as Brazil’s president, highlighting his focus on social inclusion,
articles.body: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor has welcomed Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election as Brazil’s president, highlighting his focus on social inclusion, economic justice and poverty alleviation. Tharoor said Lula’s return to power could renew attention to the concerns of the working class and economically disadvantaged sections of society.In a post on X, Tharoor described Lula’s victory as a historic moment that reaffirmed the importance of people’s participation in democracy.“From the factory floor to the global stage: @LulaOficial ’s historic victory is a powerful reminder that the heartbeat of Brazil belongs to its people. As a steadfast champion of the working class and the poor, his return to leadership breathes new life into social inclusion, economic justice, and the fight against poverty in Brazil,” he wrote.Tharoor flags possible strain in Brazil-US relationsTharoor also pointed to the potential implications of Lula’s victory for Brazil’s relationship with the United States, noting that Washington had openly supported his electoral rival, according to the news agency ANI.“It’s also a challenge for ties with Washington, which had openly backed his rival. While economic and diplomatic friction (such as recent trade and tariff tussles) is likely to persist, Lula’s fiercely independent foreign policy will continue to prioritise national sovereignty over subservience,” Tharoor said.He added that the election result reflected Brazil’s preference for social progress, democratic resilience and international cooperation at a time when right-wing political movements are gaining ground across Latin America.“Brazil has chosen a path of social progress, democratic resilience, and global cooperation. A historic and, for most, unexpected result amid the waves of rising right-wing assertion in Latin America,” he added.Lula secures another term after closely contested run-offLula, an 80-year-old former factory worker and leader of the Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT), defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro in a closely fought presidential run-off, securing another non-consecutive term in office. Neither candidate had won a sufficient majority in the first round to avoid a second vote.The victory marked a significant political comeback for Lula, who had previously lost to Bolsonaro in the first round of voting.Following his win, Lula expressed gratitude to voters, young people who had mobilised in support of democracy and those who had made efforts to cast their ballots.“My eternal gratitude to the Brazilian people, to the youth who took to the streets in defense of democracy, and to every person who made an immense effort to vote and defend the future of our country. You all move me and renew my hope,” he said.He added that the victory belonged to people committed to building a more just, sovereign and democratic Brazil.According to Al Jazeera, Lula’s victory ends a series of electoral successes by far-right candidates across Latin America, where anti-incumbency sentiment, concerns about crime and promises of closer cooperation with US President Donald Trump have featured prominently in political campaigns.Voting arrangements and post-election disputeThe election was also marked by a dispute over voting arrangements. A Supreme Court justice extended polling hours by two hours following requests from both campaigns.Lula’s campaign sought additional time after reports of restricted access to public transport in key cities prompted concerns about possible voter suppression. Bolsonaro’s campaign also requested an extension in areas affected by bad weather.Meanwhile, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat and vowed to seek the annulment of the election, alleging irregularities without presenting evidence to substantiate his claims, Brazilian media reported.Lula says Brazil is ‘no one’s backyard’Following his victory, Lula asserted that Brazil would maintain an independent position in international affairs and pledged to increase public participation in government decision-making.In a post on X, he said the campaign had helped convince voters that participating in elections was essential to protecting democracy.“We managed to convince people that voting was extremely important to safeguard democracy in Brazil. articles.title: RSPB Minsmere will never be the same after wildfire, says charity
articles.summary: Three months on from a devastating wildfire, the RSPB says it will take 20 years to recover.
articles.body:
A nature reserve has said the wildlife "will never really be the same again" after a huge wildfire almost three months ago.

The blaze, which broke out on 29 July , started on the edge of RSPB Minsmere before it spread to neighbouring Dunwich Heath on the Suffolk coast.

Firefighters have been unable to determine the cause .

Ian Barthorpe, visitor experience officer at Minsmere, said the team was concerned about the long-term implications the fire.

"It's going to be a long process of recovery of the habitat and some species like the deer and the birds have relocated to other parts of the reserve," he explained.

"But unfortunately we're really concerned about the impacts it will have on some of the invertebrates, the plants and the reptiles.

"It'll be 20 years or more before those parts of the reserve start to look like they used to."

Some trails and heathland areas of the site were hit by the fire, but fortunately wind conditions as well as the vegetation and marshland had stopped it spreading further into the reserve.

Parts of the heathland were still recording temperatures of more than 53C (127F) underground earlier this month.

Barthorpe said he had been shocked at the "apocalyptic scenes" following the fire which he said had been "quite sobering".

"It's changed the landscape so much," he continued.

"We were lucky in many ways - we didn't lose buildings, we didn't lose life or human life, but from a wildlife point of view, it will never really quite be the same again."

The main nature reserve, visitor centre and trails around its wetland areas were not affected in the fire and are all open, although the National Trust has closed Dunwich Heath and the adjoining beach to visitors.

The reserve is best known for its avocets, bitterns and other water birds, and has been a base for the BBC Springwatch programme .

Barthorpe said there was still "amazing wildlife" and "stunning scenery" for visitors to enjoy and see.

"Let's celebrate what we've got more than what we've lost and ensure that we've still got it for the future," he added.

articles.title: Mapped: Theatres at risk and fighting back across the West of England
articles.summary: During these difficult times, venues are keeping their doors open in a range of ways.
articles.body:
In the space of a week, two theatres in the West of England announced they would be closing their doors.

Taunton Brewhouse said on 7 October that it would shut at the end of the month , citing financial difficulties. A week later, Bristol Improv Theatre announced it would close with immediate effect due to its "very difficult and precarious financial position".

Other theatres across the region are having to rely on government funding, crowd funders and community takeover bids to keep their doors open.

The BBC has mapped closures and campaigns to save and revive theatres, showing a mixed picture across the region.

Teenage boy dies in crash following police pursuit

Three arrested after illegal warehouse rave

The penguins are noisy, the people fantastic - what it takes to be an Antarctic postmaster

Joshua McTaggart, chief executive of the Theatre's Trust said more smaller venues risk closing down due to rising energy bills, staff wages and the maintenance of older buildings, while audiences are "increasingly choosing to go into the city to see big productions, rather than the local theatre".

But he said there was still reason to hope that "the state of the theatre is, for the most part, buoyant".

The BBC has spoken to theatres of ranging sizes to see how they are managing to keep their doors open during these difficult times.

The Octagon Theatre in Yeovil has been shut since May 2023 after a previous larger-scale refurbishment was abandoned due to rising costs.

Somerset Council's planning committee approved a new redevelopment scheme in February , which includes making changes to the foyer and cafe, creating a new studio space and extending the backstage area.

Adam Burgan, theatre manager, said he felt "concern" and "sadness" about recent theatre closures elsewhere because of the "power and importance theatre plays in the community".

"It's a difficult time with rising utility costs, these are expensive buildings to heat and maintain," he said.

"Audiences are tightening their belts slightly due to the cost of living," he said, adding families leave it later to book.

"We're very lucky that we're having the £15m development, to make it a more efficient building to run."

After contractors are appointed, building work could start in the new year and be completed by autumn/winter 2028/29

"I can't wait to see a crane and spades in the ground and for our audiences to see a major milestone in seeing Octagon reopening," he said.

£10m of this is coming from the Arts Council and £3.75m from Yeovil Town Council, which they will have to repay with via a ticket levy.

"Theatres are often one of the heartbearts of the town, if we look at economic case we know they can drive regeneration of a town," Burgan said.

"It's also about feeling a sense of pride in the place where we live, we all need arts and culture to lift our spirits."

The Mechanics' Institute in Swindon is another venue that would need a major overhaul after closing in 1986.

The 19th Century Grade II gothic-style listed building has fallen into disrepair and been subject to break-ins and a fire in April.

But the Theatres Trust gave the Swindon Preservation Society a grant of £10,000 to carry out a new viability study exploring future visions for the building.

Lots of smaller theatres aren't so lucky to have access to large pots of government money and instead have had to rely on crowdfunding.

The Kings Theatre in Gloucester reopened last year after a huge fundraising effort by locals.

The volunteer-run venue had closed in early 2025 after an audit exposed fire safety risks, and £20,000 was raised to bring the building up to scratch.

Armstrong Hall in Thornbury, to the north of Bristol, also reopened last year after a large donation made the much-needed refurbishment possible.

After closing during Covid in 2020, a £350,000 gift from Maggie Lansdown led to renovation of one of the performance halls, as well as a new foyer, bar, toilets and green room.

The Cheltenham Playhouse is another venue to rely on a fundraising campaign to stay open.

It ran a number of fundraising initiatives in 2025 to raise its target of £100,000, with the help of a grant from Cheltenham Borough Council of £25,000.

Miles Leven, their theatre manager, said: "It always really sad to see any venues closing, big or small.

"The cost of owning and managing a premises means creative spaces are struggling to remain open.

"Audiences do want culture and live entertainment, but it's the balance of the cost and the upkeep."

He said the charity's difficult financial position was averted last year due to a fundraising campaign, allowing them to keep the doors open.

He said the theatre is working out how to combine a more commercial approach with its community and charitable aims so that it becomes more viable in future.

But the cost of maintaining the Grade-II listed building keeps going up, including £1m to fix the roof that is currently leaking onto the stage.

"No better management is going to get us to replace that roof - support is limited and it feels like it's going to have to be luck that gets us there."

Leven said they have competition from a bigger theatre on their doorstop, but "some people prefer a more intimate performance setting".

His urged audiences to support smaller venues by "trying something different".

Some venues are having to offer a variety of things due to the decline of community space.

The Amulet Theatre in Shepton Mallet closed in 2010, but after being used and a gym and unsuccessful attempts to turn it into flats, there are plans for a community takeover.

Martin Berkeley from the Buy The Amulet campaign said the town doesn't have a proper community space let alone a dedicates theatre.

"Running a commercial theatre becoming increasingly difficult," he said.

Some 300 local people have already bought shares and funding applications have been submitted to help reach the total of nearly £750,000 to buy the building.

"We would start with a community centre purpose and then add pantomimes and professional touring theatre shows," he said.

They are waiting for news on the new Community Right to Buy fund.

"Public funding is mostly aimed at existing venues, there's very little for buying buildings."

They ran a series of temporary events last summer on a "shoestring budget" and plan to eventually increase the capacity of the theatre space to make it more financially viable.

"We're still on target, we're making progress, but it's painfully slow because there's a lack of funding out there, so for now it's about remaining community focused," he said.

articles.title: The dump detectives on the trail of the illegal fly-tippers
articles.summary: The BBC joins environmental enforcement officers as they sift through illegally-dumped waste for clues.
articles.body:
A discarded microwave, a mattress sodden by the rain and even a pile of used syringes. The reality of illegally dumped waste sits before me in a colossal mound next to the side of a motorway.

For the team I'm with, this is a jigsaw waiting to be pieced together and solved as they try to identify the criminal culprits.

It does not take long for Anthony Horan and Ashley Hanley from North East Lincolnshire Council to find answers within the mountain of waste on the side of the Brocklesby Interchange near Grimsby.

"I'm gobsmacked at the amount of evidence in this one," Anthony Horan, who works as a senior environmental health practitioner for the authority.

"I'm disgusted at the needles. I've never found this amount ever."

A number of times during the interview we pause after spotting a syringe close to our feet. Some are hidden under items, others are in plain sight.

The team tells me this is exactly why they wear protective equipment.

Meanwhile, a picture starts to emerge as letters with different names and addresses - all miles outside the area - are fished out and photographed.

Horan tells me if evidence which identifies a person is found, they will be questioned.

If found liable, they could be fined if they have not properly undergone a "domestic duty of care".

"A lot of people think enviro-crime or fly-tipping is a victimless crime," Horan says. "It's not, there's many victims."

Horan says people often employ a "man with a van" to dispose of their waste, but frequently the person hired just dumps it.

If the waste is found dumped on private land, the owner will have to pay for its removal. Councils only pay if it is on public land.

Wearing thick gloves, environmental enforcement officer Hanley continues to dig through the dump.

I ask him about rogue waste removers and his advice for people wanting to get rid of waste.

"I would advise people to take the right precautions, make sure that they're giving it to somebody who has a waste carriage licence," Hanley says.

"Make sure that you're taking it to a proper waste facility if you're doing it yourself," he adds.

The Environment Agency says waste criminals "scar our environment and communities".

It says: "Illegal waste dumping is a crime that costs the public purse £1bn a year. We know the challenges and are working hard to overcome them."

It encourages the public to report suspected waste crime to its incident hotline or via its website.

In August, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said fines for fly-tipping would increase from £300 to £5,000 and offenders could be given up to nine points on their driving licence.

Across the Humber Bridge, I meet Hull City Council's Streetscene team as they arrive at a fly-tip in the middle of a housing estate.

Under this authority, the fines for fly-tipping are higher at £1,000.

As teams drag mattresses and wooden planks onto the truck, they tell a similarly frustrated story.

"It's all over the city and now it's on the rise," says Mike, one of the men clearing the waste.

"We've got a job to do so we have to clear it and move on to the next fly-tip and do the same again."

Carl Wilson, the team manager, tells me this location is a hotspot and criminals will be back soon enough.

"This will all get cleared away and then in a couple of weeks they'll probably do it again," Carl says.

"That's why you need this evidence to catch them, to stop them, to put it to a stop."

The authority tells me they often visit hotspots to deliver letters to residents on how to properly dispose of waste to prevent fly-tipping.

Back near Grimsby, I ask the North East Lincolnshire team what their message is to fly-tippers or people considering dumping their waste.

"Don't do it because we'll catch you," he says. "We don't want to be doing this, we want you to do the correct thing."
