articles.title: An Alabama father and daughter warned their insurer they feared the other might burn their $500,000 home; it went up in flames a few weeks later
articles.summary: An Alabama father and daughter warned their home insurer that they feared the other might deliberately set fire to their jointly owned property.
articles.body: An Alabama father and daughter warned their home insurer that they feared the other might deliberately set fire to their jointly owned property. Despite both warnings, USAA General Indemnity Company issued a policy covering the house for $500,000. The property in Centre, Alabama, burned down a few weeks later, leading to a dispute over whether the insurer was required to pay the claim. The case eventually reached the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, which ruled on the insurance policy and the company's decision to deny coverage.Why did the Alabama father and daughter fear their $500,000 home would burnAccording to the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit's ruling in Martin D. Renfroe v. USAA General Indemnity Co., published on 11 August 2026, the dispute involved Dennis Renfroe and his daughter, Sherry Lambert, who jointly owned the property.Their relationship had deteriorated over several years. Lambert had previously obtained a restraining order against her father and said they had not spoken outside court proceedings for 5 years. They were also involved in legal disputes over the Alabama property and a shared investment account worth $500,000.Both wanted control of the property. Just two weeks before the fire, a state court had ordered it to be sold at auction, with the proceeds to be divided between them.The court's account explained that their strained relationship had fuelled mutual suspicions about the possibility of arson. These concerns became central to the subsequent insurance dispute.Both parties raised concerns before the fireIn January 2020, before obtaining the insurance policy, Renfroe told USAA that he suspected his daughter was preparing to burn the house. He pointed to furniture being moved in and out of the property as a reason for his concern.Lambert, meanwhile, said she had removed sentimental belongings after hearing that her father and her former husband were allegedly planning to set the house on fire.The insurer subsequently issued a policy providing $500,000 in coverage for the house. Both Renfroe and Lambert were named as insured parties.According to the Eleventh Circuit's judgment, Lambert later contacted USAA after learning that her father had taken out the policy. She warned the insurer that she believed Renfroe was planning to burn the property and referred to what she described as his history involving house fires. Despite receiving warnings from both sides, USAA kept the policy in force.What happened after the house caught fireA few weeks after the insurance policy was issued, the property burned down. Renfroe submitted an insurance claim, but the subsequent investigation did not establish who had started the fire.The insurer's final investigative report did not rule out an accidental cause, although it concluded that the characteristics of the fire were consistent with arson.Both Renfroe and Lambert continued to accuse the other of responsibility. The court's ruling also recorded evidence concerning earlier fires involving properties associated with Renfroe and Lambert.Renfroe admitted during the proceedings that two previous house fires had occurred. Lambert testified about three additional fires, including one at a former home she had shared with her father.USAA ultimately denied the claim, relying on a provision in the policy that excluded losses intentionally caused by any insured person. The provision also prevented an insured person who had not caused the fire from collecting if another person covered by the same policy had deliberately caused the loss.The legal dispute therefore centred not only on who might have started the fire but also on whether the policy allowed the insurer to refuse payment to an innocent co-owner.The insurance dispute moved through the courtsRenfroe sued USAA, alleging breach of contract and bad faith in the denial of his claim.The case was heard by a federal district court in Alabama. That court concluded that the policy's innocent-insured exclusion was invalid under Alabama public policy. However, it allowed the case to proceed to trial because the insurer could still argue that Renfroe himself had caused the fire.The district court also rejected Renfroe's bad-faith claim, finding that the insurer had a legally sufficient basis to deny coverage.During the trial, both sides were permitted to present evidence suggesting that Lambert might have been responsible. However, USAA was prevented from relying on the innocent-insured exclusion as a defence.The jury awarded Renfroe $425,000. Following further proceedings, the district court reduced the amount to $226,727.85.Both parties challenged aspects of the outcome. USAA argued that the court should have allowed it to rely on the policy exclusion, while Renfroe challenged the rejection of his bad-faith claim and the denial of prejudgment interest.The appeals court allowed the insurer to rely on the exclusionThe Eleventh Circuit disagreed with the district court's conclusion that the exclusion violated Alabama public policy.In its 11 August 2026 judgment, the appeals court explained that Alabama law did not generally prohibit insurance policies from excluding coverage when an insured person intentionally caused a loss. It found no state statute or established court ruling that made the provision in Renfroe's policy invalid.The court also noted that Alabama law specifically protects innocent co-insured people in certain cases involving domestic abuse. In its view, this exception demonstrated that the state legislature could prohibit such exclusions in particular circumstances.The policy itself included an exception for innocent insured victims protected by the Domestic Abuse Insurance Protection Act.The appeals court therefore held that the exclusion was enforceable under Alabama law. This meant USAA should have been permitted to use the provision when defending its refusal to pay the claim. The ruling did not establish that either Renfroe or Lambert had started the fire.The bad-faith claim remained rejectedThe appeals court separately upheld the decision to dismiss Renfroe's bad-faith claim. It found that USAA had sufficient evidence to provide a reasonable basis for refusing the insurance payout.According to the judgment, the insurer's investigator considered the fire potentially deliberate. Other evidence included Lambert's allegation that her father might have wanted the property destroyed so he could purchase the land more cheaply at the courthouse auction.Cell tower records also suggested that Renfroe might have been near the property when the fire began. Investigators further noted that a gas line connected to a space heater had been severed before the fire. Renfroe's former work as a pipefitter was relevant to the court's consideration of that evidence.These findings did not amount to a definitive determination that Renfroe had committed arson. However, the appeals court concluded that the evidence gave USAA a sufficiently arguable reason to deny coverage, meaning its decision did not establish bad faith. articles.title: Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies aged 46
articles.summary: Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme.
articles.body:
Eric Bauza, the voice artist behind Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died aged 46.

A statement from the Emmy award-winning star's family posted on Instagram said he had died "suddenly".

Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme, and appeared in the recent release Forgotten Island.

Variety reports that the cause of death was hypertensive cardiovascular disease and that Bauza died at home on Sunday.

In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza, who was born in Ontario and was of Filipino descent, said he grew up a huge fan of the Looney Tunes characters and used to copy the voices as a child.

"Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures," he said . "It doesn't matter what part of the planet you're from. You get the comedy."

He voiced Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd and Foghorn Leghorn in 2021's Space Jam: A New Legacy before reprising those roles and that of Road Runner in Coyote vs. Acme.

He also played the part of Toad General in 2023's The Super Mario Bros. Movie and its sequel The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, the fifth highest-grossing film internationally this year.

Between 2022 and 2025, he won three Emmy awards for outstanding voice performance in a number of TV series.

In a statement reported by the Hollywood Reporter , Channing Dungey, the chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks, said: "Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world.

"He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life."

articles.title: Museum of Oxford fees partly axed after drop in footfall
articles.summary: City residents will no longer have to pay the £4 entry fee to the Museum of Oxford.
articles.body:
Controversial admission fees for a city centre museum have been partially abandoned after a reportedly sharp decline in footfall.

Oxford City Council introduced entrance fees at the Museum of Oxford in January for the first time since it opened in 1975, to fill what it said was a gap in its budget.

Since the £4 entry fee was introduced, campaign group Save Our Museum said footfall at the St Aldates attraction had fallen by 70 – 80% compared with 2024/25.

At a meeting last week, the council agreed to row back on some of the changes, with free entry being restored for Oxford residents.

"We always regretted having to introduce charges for local residents," council leader Susan Brown said.

"People should go [to the museum], and now nobody in Oxford will have an excuse not to go there because it will be free again."

The free admission for city residents will initially run as a pilot scheme from 4 January until the end of March, at which point the council will decide whether to make it permanent.

The fees were first introduced at the start of the year to fill a budget gap at the museum, which is subsidised by the city council.

Despite the gap still existing, the council's finance chief Ed Turner said: "We've listened and we've seen what we can do."

Avril Alexander, from the Save Our Museum Campaign, welcomed the move, saying the council had "made a massive mistake in introducing entry fees to a small local museum in a city full of world-renowned free ones".

"We're glad that Oxford residents' voices have been heard and those fees are now being scrapped – hopefully for good," she said.

The group now wanted the council to commit to covering the full costs of the museum "so that staff can focus on rebuilding goodwill, footfall and donations", she added.

articles.title: Lancashire dog lover says £12 tug toy from Amazon killed her pet
articles.summary: After losing her cane corso, Antonia Speariett wants to warn other dog owners about rope tug toys.
articles.body:
A heartbroken dog owner whose pet died after swallowing part of a tug toy has warned others about the dangers they can pose.

Antonia Speariett, from Coppull in Lancashire, spoke to the BBC after her five-year-old cane corso Cane died from an intestinal blockage caused by ingesting part of a toy she had bought online.

"A £12 dog toy bought from Amazon killed my dog," said the 31-year-old. "Nothing prepared me for this heartbreak. If you are a dog owner who has rope dog toys - throw them out. It is not worth it."

An Amazon spokesperson said: "We were very sorry to hear about this. We are in touch with the customer."

Antonia said she had owned Cane since he was a puppy.

"Cane was always there, like he was my protector," she said.

"Even at five years old he was like a puppy almost - so full of life."

Antonia said she knew something was wrong with him on 7 October when her 95kg (15st) pet did not eat his dinner.

"He started being a bit funny within himself," she said.

"We had been playing 'tug of war' with him holding onto a rope toy, pulling it back and forth.

"We stopped playing and he then would not eat his tea."

When Cane again refused food the following day, Antonia took him to the vet.

Cane was diagnosed with an intestinal blockage and needed emergency surgery.

Antonia said she suspected the rope toy could be to blame and her worst fears were soon confirmed.

"The vet called us and said they had opened him up and were looking at the rope toy," Antonia said.

"It had anchored in his stomach and was in his intestines - wrapped around like cheese wire.

"The vet said the rope had cut off blood supply to Cane's intestines and they had gone a black and dark purple colour.

"We were told the blood supply wasn't returning.

"I broke down and was begging the vet 'is there anything that can be done to save him'," Antonia said.

"But there wasn't. We had 15 minutes to get back to the vets to say goodbye."

In the space of only two days, Antonia said she had gone from having a young "full of life" dog to bidding her beloved Cane goodbye.

Antonia said she wanted to raise awareness of the potential dangers of rope dog toys so no owner has to go through what she has.

"Cane was not a small dog," she explained. "He was 5ft 2in and he was a unit.

Since sharing Cane's story on social media, Antonia said she had discovered many other dog owners with similar experiences.

"The amount of people that have come forward and said this happened to our dog - there are so many," she said.

"And it is not just one brand or seller."

Antonia has launched a petition calling for further legislation surrounding the safety of dog toys.

She added: "I decided I needed to do something for Cane so this doesn't happen again."

articles.title: Wolverhampton shopping centre to be turned into giant art canvas
articles.summary: Hundreds of people will help turn Wolverhampton's Mander Centre into a giant public artwork.
articles.body:
Later this month, hundreds of people will be invited to turn a shopping centre into one giant canvas to help celebrate their city.

The Mander Centre in Wolverhampton will host a three-day celebration of drawing between 27 and 29 October as part of a collaboration between the University of Wolverhampton and The Big Draw.

The Big Draw is an annual international celebration that has reached more than five million people, in more than 35 countries, since launching in 2000.

Led by practitioners from Fine Art and Illustration within the university's School of Creative Industries, people will work together to create an evolving large-scale drawing inspired by Wolverhampton.

Participants will be encouraged to respond to the people, architecture, stories and experiences that help shape the city.

Organisers said the artwork would grow and evolve over the three days as more people added their own ideas, memories and perspectives.

The project is inspired by psychogeography, a concept that explores people's connections with places and how they experience their surroundings.

Lindsey Chambers, head of School of Social Science, Humanities and Creative Industries at the university, said: "Over three days, we hope to see the artwork grow and evolve as more people add their own ideas and perspectives.

"You don't need any previous drawing experience to get involved. We want everyone to feel welcome to come along, have a go and make their mark."

This year's Big Draw theme is "Make a Mark", which celebrates drawing as a form of exploration and expression.

The University of Wolverhampton is one of the festival's partners for 2026, alongside organisations including the National Trust, St Paul's Cathedral, the Wallace Collection, the Courtauld Gallery and the Quentin Blake Centre for Illustration.

Matilda Barratt, director of The Big Draw, said organisers were grateful to the organisations helping deliver events around the world as part of the festival.

The event is free to attend, with all materials provided and opportunities to take part through both scheduled activities and informal drop-in sessions.

articles.title: Bristol woman wins £127k High Court claim for mum's care at home
articles.summary: Bern Rogers says the row with her siblings since her elderly mother died was "harrowing and deeply sad".
articles.body:
A woman has described her "phenomenal" relief after she won a legal case that means she is entitled to be paid for caring for her elderly mother in her final years.

Bern Rogers, from Bristol, told the BBC of the "harrowing and deeply sad" family dispute since her elderly mother Sheila died in 2020, which even led to her facing criminal charges.

Legal experts said the "hugely significant" High Court ruling would lead to other claims.

The executor of Sheila's estate, Bern's brother Andrew, said it had "always been willing to pay" her "genuine expenses" and an extra amount for her efforts. But the estate intends to appeal against the judgment that awarded Bern £127,500 for care she provided.

Bern looked after Sheila, who had dementia, for two-and-a-half years.

After Sheila moved into Bern's house in Bristol in September 2017, she wanted to be cared for by her daughter rather than get costly home care or go into a residential care home.

Crucially, Bern said she agreed with her mother she would be paid for the round-the-clock care.

After Sheila died in April 2020, Bern took £100,000 from her estate. It led to her being reported to the police for fraud and theft.

The money was seized and Bern was charged. But, at a trial at Bristol Crown Court in 2022, she was found not guilty by a jury.

After being cleared, Bern turned to the civil courts.

In 2025, a High Court judge ruled she had entered into an informal contract with Sheila for payment of a reasonable sum for her care.

The estate was also ordered by a judge to pay Bern's legal costs.

In August this year, another High Court judge worked out the amount Bern was due and ruled she was owed £127,500 for the 850 days of care she provided.

"Mum came to live with me, she became very confused and was seen wandering in the garden and obviously needed care," Bern said. "We didn't know what was wrong with her."

She said caring for her mother had been like a full-time job, adding: "I couldn't leave her really. She became unpredictable."

Sheila became more frail, was diagnosed with dementia and also had a series of physical health problems, including a "chronic" and "disabling" prolapse.

Bern's husband John said: "It was relentless after she moved in with us. We couldn't go out even to the shops. It was a 24-hour job.

"It was a privilege, but we had to put our lives on hold for more than two years and revolve our lives around looking after her."

He remembered that in Sheila's final weeks, his wife was sleeping on the floor of her mother's bedroom to make sure she was alright.

Bern said "of course" she would have looked after her mother if she had not been able to pay her.

But she said her mother had wanted to be looked after by her daughter rather than getting professional carers or going into a home, which would have cost thousands of pounds a month.

"She was very insistent and would tell anyone that would listen that she wanted to make sure that I sorted out money for her care, I was to make sure I got paid properly," she said.

Multiple messages from Bern's five siblings were shown in court saying that she should be paid something for the care, although no amount was agreed.

That is why, she explained, shortly after her mother had died, she transferred £100,000 from her mother's account.

Bern was reported to the police for theft and fraud, which she describes as a "terrible and devastating betrayal".

"It has been harrowing and deeply sad for it to go from a normal family relationship to being treated like a scapegoat, five against one," she said.

After the two separate High Court judgements in her favour, Bern said: "The weight off my shoulders was phenomenal.

"It has been absolutely wonderful to be vindicated. It means I can get on with my life now, the rest of my retirement."

Bern said: "I'm very proud of her, actually, because she has stuck up for her mother, for carers and for herself.

"It's been a very long and tough journey of nine years, and we've finally got justice."

Legal experts have told the BBC that while this case does not automatically set a legal precedent, it is likely to lead to similar claims in future.

Emma Holland, partner in trust and litigation at Stewarts, said: "What this case demonstrates is that the courts are willing to apply ordinary contractual principles to family relationships, which wasn't clear before."

This means family members are more likely to be entitled to payment if there is an informal agreement, she said, even without an amount being agreed.

"These are considered, well-reasoned judgements by highly esteemed judges, so I would think it's very likely that future courts will follow them," Holland said.

Beth Middleton, senior associate in private wealth and disputes at JMW, said this was a "hugely significant" case that would "open a floodgate of claims".

Sarama Dutton, partner at Collyer and Bristow, who specialises in trusts, inheritance and wills, said the judgements were likely to be "influential".

"It demonstrates a willingness to look beyond individual care tasks and acknowledges the broader reality of providing care to an elderly relative, including the continuous supervision, responsibility and restrictions on personal freedom," she said.

Bern said she was "terribly proud" that her case could influence others in future, which she said was her mum's "legacy".

"It's a huge win for carers everywhere," John added, but stressed families still needed to have open discussions about what was fair.

The ruling that states that Bern is entitled to payment cannot be appealed against, however, the estate intends to lodge an appeal against the second ruling that decided the amount owed.

The executor of Sheila's estate is Bern's brother, Andrew Wills. In a statement on behalf of the estate, he said: "The only agreements that we (her siblings) were aware of was for my mother to give Bernadette £50 per week 'keep' and to ensure that Bernadette was not to be out of pocket.

"We were not made aware of any other contract between our mother and Bernadette."

The statement added: "At all times I have attempted to be independent and to act in the best interests of the estate.

"The estate has always been willing to pay Bernadette her genuine expenses as well as an additional gratuity in recognition of her efforts for our mother.

"We have always tried to be fair. Unfortunately, our offers were not accepted by Bernadette who instead issued legal proceedings against the estate."

articles.title: Legally Blonde at 25: Lawyers inspired by Reese Witherspoon's Elle Woods
articles.summary: Twenty five years after the release of Legally Blonde in the UK, lawyers discuss how the film inspired them
articles.body:
It has been 25 years since Elle Woods stomped her 'last season Prada shoes' across UK screens in Legally Blonde.

The film, which was released 25 years ago today, sees Woods played by Reese Witherspoon , enrol in Harvard Law School after her boyfriend dumps her for not being serious enough. The film went on to inspire generations of would-be lawyers and solicitors.

A quarter of a century later, women now outnumber men in the legal industry. And while "the Legally Blonde effect" may not be the sole reason for the boost, lawyers say it has not hurt the cause.

"It definitely inspired the kind of lawyer I wanted to be," trainee solicitor Olivia Holder said.

Olivia, who works for Manchester-based Express Solicitors, said she believes people's access to justice can improve when solicitors are free to be themselves.

"I love to wear pink, I've got a pink sparkly car and I didn't have to give up any of that to be taken seriously in the legal profession," she said.

And in the same way Elle uses her knowledge of perm aftercare to prove her client's innocence, Olivia believes her interests helps her advocate for her clients.

"Sometimes we're dealing with clients who have scarring and they say things like, 'Oh, it might sound silly, but I'm concerned about the way I look,' and I say 'No, it doesn't sound silly at all.' I can empathise with that," the 24-year-old from Macclesfield said.

According to the Solicitors Regulation Authority, in 2001, the year Legally Blonde was released, 43% of solicitors in England and Wales were women. As of last year, women made up 63% of solicitors the Law Society found.

However, Deputy Vice President of the society Dana Denis-Smith, said many women still feel like they do not belong.

"My whole legal career tracks Legally Blonde because I started my legal education 25 years ago, about three months after it came out," the 51-year-old from the Transylvania region of Romania said.

"Previous to this film, a lot of the women in law portrayed in film were very hard women. They had to play hardball."

Dana said women have only been able practice law since around 1922. And when the first generation entered the profession they faced ridicule and questions around what they would wear and how they would behave, as well as discrimination around the types of work they could do.

"It was about what was considered suitable for a woman," she said.

"Legally Blonde broke with that tradition of 'you can't be feminine and successful'. I think it was a very pivotal moment for women.

"Before you would hide away your children and not talk about your family life. There was a sense that you had to really separate your professional identity," she added.

Solicitor Lois Ellard, said she appreciates the way the film challenges the stereotype that people who care about their appearance cannot do a difficult job.

"Elle is obviously perceived as this bimbo sort of girl. And then she goes to Harvard and I just think it's amazing," the 28-year-old from Pontefract in West Yorkshire said.

"I get my lashes done, I get my brows done, I get my hair done, I tan, I bleach my teeth, I have lip filler. All things some people think don't go hand-in-hand with being a solicitor. But here I am.

"One of my favourite things is when I'm on a night out and people try to guess what I do and nobody ever guesses solicitor.

"I just think the look on people's faces and I'm like, 'Yeah, I'm a solicitor, why wouldn't you think that?'I love that," Lois who works for Manchester-based Express Solicitors said.

While Lamya Al Saqqaf, a trainee solicitor at MSB solicitors in Liverpool, said she is inspired by the way that Elle uses the fact that she is constantly underestimated as a source of motivation.

"When you put your mind to something, you can see it through and I think the movie is a perfect example of that for many women," she said.

However, she said fans cannot ignore that if the character were from a black, Asian and minority ethnic background she may not be able to access law school so easily.

In England and Wales 75% of solicitors are white, Asian/Asian British solicitors make up 13% of the industry and Black/Black British solicitors make up just 3%, according to the Solicitors Regulation Authority.

"We don't all have the same accessibility as counterparts from white backgrounds," the 27-year-old who was born and lived in Yemen for 11 years said.

She said research by the SRA also found that white students are almost twice as likely to be sponsored by a law firm through law school than Asian and black students.

"So if they were to remake the film, seeing those issues integrated into one character would be a better representation," she said.

The gender split in the legal industry is also reflected at the University of Manchester, where female law students outnumber males 62%-38%.

Dihasya Wijewickreme Perera is in her third year studying law at the university. The 20-year-old also cheerleads for the school and said she loves that Elle kept up her hobbies after she started at Harvard.

"She's really true to herself and her interests. She does her Bachelors in fashion merchandising and that's a huge passion she carries through law school and her legal career," Dihasya said.

She said the relationship Elle has with her friends is also reflected in her female-heavy cohort at university.

"She's super positive, she has her sisterhood and her sorority, and they're all rooting for her. I think that's really lovely."

And while things have improved for women in the legal industry since 2001, experts say there is still more to be done.

Men still outnumber women in Partner positions 57%-40%, according to the SRA.

And In 2024, six in 10 female solicitors who left the role were under 55, compared to just three in 10 male solicitors of the same age.

And Dana Denis-Smith believes seeing successful, older lawyers reflected in films could help address the issues behind the statistics.

"We haven't yet seen a senior partner being depicted on film. We've always had more junior lawyer being represented," she said.

"So maybe we need that kind of more powerful, more influential voice as well to be visible as a player in the profession."

articles.title: Plans to create a wildflower meadow in King's Lynn take shape
articles.summary: Fairstead Recreation Ground is being planted with wildflowers to benefit insects and pollinators.
articles.body:
A project to transform a recreation ground into a wildflower meadow has taken another step forward.

Members of the Nature Volunteer Network and staff from the Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk have planted hundreds of native wildflower plugs in Fairstead Recreation Ground in King's Lynn.

The council said it wanted to establish a diverse mix of wildflower species to enhance the meadow and support local wildlife.

"Every plug planted brings us one step closer to establishing a thriving meadow," said Michael de Whalley, the cabinet member for climate change and biodiversity at the authority.

"[It will] benefit bees, butterflies, birds, and countless other species."

The authority said the wildflower meadow project, which followed the introduction of green hay in the area earlier this year, was one of its first practical initiatives to protect and restore habitats for insects and other wildlife across the borough.

Chris Walker, the biodiversity officer at the borough council, said: "We will be able to take what we learn from this project to recreate wildflower meadows in other areas of the borough, fitting in with our long-term investment in nature."

Wildflower meadows are among the UK's most valuable habitats , supporting a wide range of insects and wildlife while helping to connect fragmented natural spaces.

The council said once fully established, the Fairstead Recreation Ground meadow would provide food, shelter and breeding opportunities for numerous species.

It added it would continue to monitor the site's progress as the meadow develops, with the aim of creating a self-sustaining habitat to support biodiversity and potentially provide seed and plant material for future meadow creation projects elsewhere in the borough.

articles.body: Adam James, a 23-year-old autistic man from High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, has been offered a DJ set at Boomtown Fair in 2027 after attending the music festival alone and befriending a group of strangers. The aspiring drum and bass DJ met the group when they asked whether he had a mallet to help put up their tents before inviting him to camp with them. His father, Andy, later shared a social media post thanking the “lads from Bristol”, which was seen by millions. The story caught the attention of Boomtown Fair's co-founder, leading to the invitation.How did strangers help him land a dream DJ setAdam described how meeting the group helped him feel more comfortable during his first festival experience. Speaking to the BBC, he said: “I wasn't very confident in myself, but as soon as I was with them, I was fine.” He also explained why their decision to include him had meant so much to him, adding: “They could have just ignored me, but the fact they saw I was on my own and took me in was just amazing.”His father subsequently shared a post expressing his gratitude to the group, referring to them as the “lads from Bristol”. The post was shared widely online, with the BBC reporting that it had been seen by millions of people. The story also led to Adam being reunited with the group at the Trident Pub in Bristol. Following the attention surrounding his experience, he was booked for several gigs, marking further opportunities to perform as a DJ.Why was Adam invited to Boomtown Fair 2027Adam's story also reached the organisers of Boomtown Fair. The festival's co-founder, Luke Mitchell, commented on a BBC video about the story, saying it had “circled the Boomtown office with absolute joy”. He also highlighted the importance of festivals in bringing people together, stating: “Stories like this are why festivals are so incredibly important.” Mitchell then asked Adam's father: “Can we fix up a DJ set for Adam next year?”A spokesperson for Boomtown Fair subsequently confirmed that Adam had been asked to play a set at the 2027 festival. According to the BBC, the stage and performance times will be announced once programming for next year's event has begun. The invitation followed the public response to Adam's experience and his growing opportunities to perform at music events. His set will give him the chance to appear at the festival where he first met the group who welcomed him.How did Adam's story open new DJ opportunitiesThe response to Adam's story extended beyond the festival invitation. The BBC reported that he had received numerous offers from DJs and clubs inviting him to attend their events and perform at their venues. He was also invited by the Pete Tong Academy to join a DJing course, providing another opportunity to develop his skills in the field of music.His father said the response had been particularly meaningful because Adam had faced cruel comments online in the past. Speaking to the BBC, Andy said: “He's become very resilient, but he's such a lovely bloke.” He added: “It means so much to me and his Mum too.” Andy also described the public reaction as “absolutely amazing” to see and said he had watched his son's dreams come true. articles.title: Israel’s election: The main issues in the words of the leading candidates
articles.summary: From judicial reform to conscription, here’s where candidates stand on the key issues dominating the campaign.
articles.body:
For an election often billed as the most consequential in Israel’s history, many issues that outsiders might expect to divide the candidates are, in fact, points of consensus among the frontrunners.

None of the leading contenders in Tuesday’s election has questioned the case for unleashing a genocide on Gaza in response to the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, or the wars that have followed, including the one on Iran. Nor have most candidates for the premiership offered a clear path towards implementing a two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict that was envisaged in the 1990s, or towards an equitable settlement with the Palestinians whose territory Israel occupies.

Instead, the points of division centre almost exclusively on Israel’s internal politics and how voters see the future character of their country. The choice is between the hard-right government of incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, unconstrained by the judicial oversight he has railed against, and the future outlined by the disparate coalition of his opponents, which promises a broadly similar policy agenda but within the confines of the law and without the more extreme elements of the current governing coalition.

So, what have the leading candidates said about the main issues?

Despite having committed to working towards a two-state solution in the 1990s’ Oslo Accords, with many of their allies adjusting their policies towards Israel to reflect that commitment, few of the contenders in Tuesday’s election appear ready to honour it. Instead, their government stands widely accused of abetting the settler pogroms now raging across the West Bank, while supporting continued construction in the occupied territory in defiance of international law. This includes the E1 settlement plan , which ministers openly boast will bury the two-state solution.

Here’s what some of the contenders have said:

Likud party leader, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu : “We are going to fulfill our promise that there will be no Palestinian state; this place belongs to us.”

Yashar party Gadi Eisenkot : “My position on the Palestinian issue has remained consistent: The principle of two states for two peoples is a mistake.”

Religious Zionist party leader, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich : The next government should “destroy the idea of an Arab terror state; finally, formally and practically cancel the cursed Oslo Accords and get on the path of sovereignty, while encouraging migration both from Gaza and from Judea and Samaria [occupied West Bank]. There is no other long-term solution.”

The Democrats leader Yair Golan : “We need to understand that Israeli society is still in trauma from October 7. To make the galactic leap from the current situation to a two-state solution is impossible. It’s not enough to return to old formulas, we need to adjust our plans, our ideas, our perceptions. My concept is about civil separation and security responsibility.”

The conscription of Israel’s growing ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, population into the army is an issue largely unique to Israel, and one whose prominence has grown as the human and economic costs of the wars in which many refuse to take part have mounted.

Netanyahu has continued to rely on the two main Haredi parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), for support in the Knesset. They have in turn insisted that he pass legislation overturning the Supreme Court ruling of June 25, 2024 and offering ultra-Orthodox youth a legislative shield against conscription.

Netanyahu after the arrest this month of about 40 Haredim – plural for Haredi – for avoiding the draft: “We must preserve the world of Torah because it preserved us. These arrests are a deliberate attempt to harm the process of drafting Haredim without coercion.”

Shas leader Aryeh Deri : “There will be no government in Israel with Shas’s support or participation unless the status of yeshiva [seminary] students is regulated.”

Eisenkot : “That is what the upcoming election is about: Netanyahu’s draft-dodging government, or a government of conscription led by me.”

Yisrael Beiteinu party leader Avigdor Liberman : “Netanyahu is issuing an impassioned call against the arrest of draft evaders, once again proving that he is a hostage to the draft evaders – without them, he has no government.”

Days after taking office in 2022, Netanyahu’s government unveiled a plan to curb the powers of Israel’s courts, which triggered months of mass protests in 2023 before the war on Gaza paused the fight.

The coalition has passed measures reshaping how judges are appointed, while in July a law stripped Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara of many of her powers, allowing the government to reject her legal advice and choose its own lawyers in court. Both are due to take effect after the election and most of the opposition has promised to reverse them.

The government has also boycotted Chief Justice Isaac Amit. Critics call it a deliberate assault on democracy by a prime minister embroiled in a long-running corruption trial of his own, while Justice Minister Yariv Levin says the election is a historic chance to finish the job.

Here are some of the contenders’ statements:

Netanyahu : “Democracy is the rule of the people. It’s ‘we the people,’ not ‘we the judges … In Israel, [judicial reform] was completely derailed, and we have to bring it back. We don’t have to crush the judiciary, but we have to make sure it doesn’t crush the legislative branch, the Knesset or the executive branch of government.”

Together alliance co-leader, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett : “I want to be clear. We will cancel all the legal revolution laws immediately upon the convening of the Knesset.”

While the killing of more than 74,000 people in Gaza has been entirely absent during the campaign of the two main alliances, questions over political accountability for security failures ahead of and during the Hamas-led attack in 2023 have dominated this election cycle.

Inquiries into failings by the security services ahead of and during the Hamas-led attack led to the resignation of Chief of Staff Herzi Halevi , announced in January 2025. They also fed a long, drawn-out and bitter fight with the prime minister that ended with the departure of Shin Bet head Ronen Bar in June last year.

However, despite recent news reports suggesting that Netanyahu was warned by both the UAE and Egypt ahead of the attack, and longstanding criticism of his policy of keeping Hamas in power in Gaza as a bulwark against the Palestinian Authority, no similar inquiry into his own alleged failings before October 7 has happened.

Here are some of the leaders’ statements:

Eisenkot : “Netanyahu was warned and did not act. A State Commission of Inquiry that we will establish will investigate the disaster. The heads of the systems took responsibility and resigned long ago. We will not allow the master of evaders to escape the truth.”

Netanyahu : The prime minister told the Knesset that his government “wants to establish a commission of inquiry with as broad public support as possible” and not one dismissed by what he claimed is “at least half the country”. The proposed government-led inquiry never reached its final reading and has been deferred to the next session.

articles.title: Photos: Lula supporters flood streets in celebration of historic win
articles.summary: Avenues and squares in Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo filled with crowds dressed in red, celebrating democracy.
articles.body:
Fireworks lit up the night sky in Brazilian cities as supporters of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva poured into the streets to celebrate his dramatic re-election victory on Sunday.

In Rio de Janeiro, vuvuzelas echoed along the beachfront and central avenues as crowds draped in Brazil’s green-and-yellow flag and Lula’s trademark red danced, sang campaign songs and chanted pro-democracy slogans.

In Sao Paulo, thousands of people dressed in red, the colour of Lula’s Workers’ Party, packed central squares and major roads, waving banners and setting off flares in scenes reminiscent of football title celebrations.

According to official results, Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, secured an unprecedented fourth term with 51.8 percent of the vote against 48.2 percent for his far-right rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. Lula hailed the high turnout, saying Brazilians had “voted to defend democracy”.

The jubilation unfolded despite Bolsonaro’s refusal to accept the result, promising to seek to annul the vote after a Supreme Court decision extended polling by two hours.

But in city after city, Lula’s supporters treated the win as a resounding repudiation of authoritarianism and a renewed mandate for Brazil’s left.

Joyful cheers of "Let's go, Lula!" rose from the jubilant crowd again and again as Brazilians paraded down Sao Paulo's Paulista Avenue on Sunday, celebrating the left-wing leader's dramatic election win. [Brian Snyder/Reuters]
Fireworks boomed and cars honked their horns as the crowd marched down Sao Paulo's main avenue. [Diego Vara/Reuters]
Thousands of people spilled onto the streets following President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's victory over his right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro. [Miguel Schincariol/AFP]
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, joined the parade, leaning out of the sunroof of his car with a megaphone in his hand and his trademark rasp more hoarse than ever. [Natacha Pisarenko/AP Photo]
Lula received 51.8 percent of the vote compared to 48.2 percent for former president Jair Bolsonaro's son, who has called for the result to be annulled. [Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo]

articles.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ surges with $19.5M at box office; ‘Clayface’ takes No. 1
articles.summary: DC Studios scored a modest, R-rated win with “Clayface,” landing a $24 million opening weekend, according to studio estimates Sunday.
articles.body: DC Studios scored a modest, R-rated win with “Clayface,” landing a $24 million opening weekend, according to studio estimates Sunday. But the biggest success story in theaters remained A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” which pulled in $19.5 million in its first weekend of wide release. The Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim-directed “You Can See Everything” increased from 855 locations to 2,655. In expansion, it continued to blow away expectations. With $45.1 million in two weeks, it already ranks among the highest-grossing documentaries ever. “You Can See Everything” has turned into a sensation partly by drawing waves of Gen Z moviegoers. Its awards season prospects are also growing. If “You Can See Everything” is nominated for best picture at the Oscars, it would be the first documentary nominated for Hollywood’s top prize. “A24 invested a reported $7 million in an interesting but complicated idea without a beginning, middle or end, that’s turned into a zeitgeist film about money, dreams, truth and reality,” said David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. ‘Clayface’ succeeds on a smaller scale for DC In 3,458 theaters, Warner Bros.’ “Clayface” narrowly edged the A24 release for first place. That’s a solid start for the Gotham City villain tale and the third theatrical release for DC under the stewardship of James Gunn and Peter Safran. A bid to meld body horror with a comic book movie, it stars Tom Rhys Harries as Matt Hagen, a rising movie star who undergoes an experimental facial surgery after a mob boss disfigures him. While such an opening would have been a flop for most superhero films, “Clayface” was budgeted at only $44 million — a fraction of the expense of most comic book films. It added $19 million internationally. That was enough to offer some stability, and assured profitability, to DC Studios following the disappointment of “Supergirl.” Earlier this year, that film grossed just $126 million worldwide on a $170 million production budget. Audiences gave “Clayface” an “A-” CinemaScore, a high grade for a horror release. Reviews were also largely good. The competition for horror audiences can be fierce in October, but “Clayface” may end up the top genre draw of the month. “Clayface is a great example of studios taking chances, with DC venturing into R-rated horror and body horror, something that’s certainly not your typical comic book movie,” said Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends for Rentrak. Last weekend’s top film, the video game adaptation “Street Fighter,” sank like a stone, dropping 72% with $8.6 million in its second weekend. The Paramount Pictures release, made for about $80 million, has grossed $46.9 million domestically in two weeks. ‘Wildwood’ and ‘Wicker’ make strong starts “Wildwood,” the latest stop-motion animated film from the Portland, Oregon-based studio Laika, debuted in third place with $11.8 million in 2,779 locations. The film, directed by Laika chief executive Travis Knight, rode excellent reviews and strong audience scores (an “A” CinemaScore) to a notable improvement over the studio’s previous release: 2019’s “The Missing Link” (a $5.9 million opening). But “Wildwood” is still unlikely to generate a profit, given that it cost $100 million to make. The PG-13 fantasy follows a teenage girl who enters an enchanted forest to find her abducted baby brother. “Wicker,” a comic fable starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård, launched with an excellent $5.8 million in 1,471 theaters. Acquired for $2.5 million out of Sundance by Black Bear Pictures, the well-reviewed “Wicker” is a quirky love story about a fisherwoman (Colman) who has the local basket maker weave her a husband (Skarsgård). The weekend’s other new releases were either hard to find or little seen. Taika Waititi’s critically panned “Klara and the Sun,” adapted from Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel, made just $725,000 at 880 theaters for Sony Pictures. Amazon MGM opted not to even report grosses for Sacha Baron Cohen’s poorly received mockumentary “Ali G: Who Iz I?” Though Cohen took the rare step of conducting numerous interviews as himself, and not in character, “Ali G: Who Iz I?” was almost absent on its opening weekend. The film’s theatrical footprint was shrunk considerably as Cohen faced backlash in the U.K. over cultural appropriation and racial caricatures. Top 10 movies by domestic box office With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak: 1. “Clayface,” $24 million. 2. “You Can See Everything,” $19.5 million. 3. “Wildwood,” $11.8 million. 4. “Street Fighter,” $8.6 million. 5. “Wicker,” $5.8 million. 6. “Other Mommy,” $3.9 million. 7. “Sense and Sensibility,” $3.4 million. 8. “Whalefall,” $3.2 million. 9. “Verity,” $3.1 million. 10. “Resident Evil,” $3 million.

articles.title: SIT formed to probe accident involving vehicles behind Rahul Gandhi’s convoy in Sultanpur
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: The Uttar Pradesh Police have constituted a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to investigate the accident involving vehicles travelling behind
articles.body: LUCKNOW: The Uttar Pradesh Police have constituted a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to investigate the accident involving vehicles travelling behind Congress leader and Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi’s convoy during his visit to Sultanpur on Monday.The SIT has been formed on the directions of the Uttar Pradesh Director General of Police (DGP) to conduct a comprehensive inquiry into the incident, establish the circumstances leading to the collision and examine possible negligence or security lapses.The three-member team will be headed by Kiran S, Inspector General of Police, Lucknow Range. Additional superintendent of police, Sultanpur, Brij Narayan Singh, and deputy superintendent of police (Traffic), Sultanpur, Ram Krishna Chaturvedi, are the other members of the team.According to a press note issued by the Uttar Pradesh Police Headquarters on Monday, the SIT will investigate the causes and circumstances of the accident and examine whether there were any lapses in security, escort arrangements or traffic management during the convoy’s movement.The team will also recommend measures to prevent the recurrence of similar incidents in the future.The police headquarters has directed the SIT to conduct a comprehensive investigation into all aspects of the incident and submit a detailed report at the earliest.The accident occurred when vehicles travelling behind Rahul Gandhi’s convoy collided while he was travelling from Lucknow towards Sultanpur.Further details regarding the circumstances of the collision are expected to emerge during the investigation.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: Hulk Hogan bought a Clearwater beachfront mansion for $3.3 million in 2012; after it was listed for nearly $11 million, his estate sold it for $5.9 million in October 2026, while a separate cottage fetched $2.8 million
articles.summary: The estate of late professional wrestling star Hulk Hogan has sold his longtime Clearwater Beach mansion for $5.9 million, more than a year after his
articles.body: The estate of late professional wrestling star Hulk Hogan has sold his longtime Clearwater Beach mansion for $5.9 million, more than a year after his death at the property in Florida. The beachfront residence initially entered the market for nearly $11 million in January 2026 before undergoing several price reductions, according to TMZ, Realtor.com and the Tampa Bay Business Journal. A separate cottage next door, also owned by Hogan, has sold for $2.8 million. The two transactions bring the reported combined sale value of the neighbouring properties to $8.7 million, although it remains unclear whether both homes were purchased by the same buyer.From a $3.3 million purchase to a multimillion-dollar saleHogan, whose real name was Terry Gene Bollea, purchased the larger property in April 2012 for approximately $3.33 million, according to property records cited by Realtor.com. Located on Clearwater Beach, the three-storey residence offers direct access to the Gulf of Mexico and expansive waterfront views. The roughly 5,400-square-foot home has five bedrooms and five-and-a-half bathrooms. Its primary suite alone spans approximately 1,000 square feet, with a sitting area, a terrace overlooking the Gulf, a morning bar, a spa-style bathroom and a large walk-in wardrobe.Other features include a private elevator, a swimming pool and spa, and extensive outdoor entertaining areas. The Mediterranean-style residence was built in 2009 and became one of the two adjoining waterfront properties Hogan owned in Clearwater. The $5.9 million sale price is substantially below the property’s initial asking price of $10.98 million. After listing in January, the mansion underwent multiple reductions as it remained on the market. By September, its asking price had fallen to $6.9 million, according to Realtor.com. The final sale price was therefore about $5.1 million below the original asking price.The neighbouring cottage sells for $2.8 millionThe mansion was not the only property from Hogan’s Clearwater holdings to change hands. The wrestler had also acquired the smaller home next door in 2016 for approximately $1.6 million, using it primarily as a guesthouse. The 2,062-square-foot cottage was subsequently listed separately, with an initial asking price of $4.5 million. It features three bedrooms, two-and-a-half bathrooms and a modern interior, along with outdoor amenities that take advantage of its coastal setting.The cottage’s reported $2.8 million sale represents a significant reduction from its original asking price as well. The two properties were marketed independently, and no public information has established whether the transactions involved a single buyer. Together, the sales mark the transfer of the two neighbouring homes that formed part of Hogan’s Florida property holdings.A sale more than a year after Hogan’s deathHogan died on July 24, 2025, at the age of 71 after suffering a medical emergency at his Clearwater residence. He was later pronounced dead at a local hospital. The mansion was subsequently listed for sale in January 2026 as his estate began marketing the property.The wrestler, widely recognised for his role in transforming professional wrestling into mainstream entertainment, had spent his later years in the Florida home. Its waterfront location, private beach access and extensive amenities were among the features highlighted in the property’s marketing. Martha Thorn of the Thorn Collection at Coldwell Banker Realty handled the listing. Thorn was a longtime friend of Hogan, according to TMZ’s report on the sale.What the final sale figures revealThe mansion’s sale for $5.9 million represents a substantial difference from its initial asking price, despite the property having been purchased for approximately $3.33 million in 2012. The cottage, meanwhile, sold for $2.8 million after entering the market at $4.5 million.The combined reported sale price of $8.7 million reflects the value achieved by the estate across both properties. However, the final proceeds cannot be determined from the sale prices alone, as transaction costs, taxes and other expenses may affect the amount received. With both properties now reported sold, the Clearwater beachfront homes that once formed Hogan’s adjoining residential compound have reached a new chapter, with ownership passing from the estate to buyers whose identities have not been publicly confirmed.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Officials from Mecca pact states to hold talks in Iran amid regional tensions
articles.summary: Talks to be first high-level contact between Iran and the bloc since Houthi rebels escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia.
articles.body:
Delegations from the Mecca Defence Alliance countries – Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan – will visit Tehran for talks, according to Saudi and Iranian officials.

Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, was quoted by state-run media as saying Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, Pakistani military chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will participate in a joint meeting during their visit to Tehran on Monday.

The Iranian delegation will be led by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council.

The participating countries could take an effective step towards establishing regional security based on actors in the region, Bagheri Kani said.

Rayed Krimly, the Saudi deputy minister for public diplomacy, also confirmed the meeting, adding that the visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Mecca Defence Alliance allies “for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis and promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions in support of the mediation efforts carried out” by Qatar and Pakistan.

“The visit underscores the pivotal role of Mecca Joint Defence Agreement countries in reinforcing regional security and stability and working with all countries in the region to achieve that goal,” he wrote on X.

The planned talks would be the first high-level contact between Iran and all members of the alliance since Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi armed group escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia last month.

Field Marshal Munir last week visited Tehran, where he met President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials.

During the visit, Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with the United States about ending the US-Israel war on Iran until Tehran’s demands were met, according to Iranian media.

Pakistan has been a key intermediary between Washington and Tehran since the US and Israel launched the war in February.

Earlier mediation efforts helped produce an interim agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the US resumed weeks later.

Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the Houthis continued.

Ministers from the Mecca Defence Alliance countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh this month and agreed to ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

The Houthi attacks have become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli war on Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠in the wider war.

Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August. Under it, an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

The agreement’s first article says the parties shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and internationally recognised borders, according to the text publicised at the time.

Efforts by Turkiye’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still under way while Pakistan approved the pact last week.
